This section should help you:

understand how to install and use the KubeRay operator.
understand how to deploy a Ray Serve application using a RayService.
understand how to monitor and update your application.
Deploying Ray Serve on Kubernetes provides the scalable compute of Ray Serve and operational benefits of Kubernetes. This combination also allows you to integrate with existing applications that may be running on Kubernetes. When running on Kubernetes, use the RayService controller from KubeRay.

NOTE: Anyscale is a managed Ray solution that provides high-availability, high-performance autoscaling, multi-cloud clusters, spot instance support, and more out of the box.
A RayService CR encapsulates a multi-node Ray Cluster and a Serve application that runs on top of it into a single Kubernetes manifest. Deploying, upgrading, and getting the status of the application can be done using standard kubectl commands. This section walks through how to deploy, monitor, and upgrade the Text ML example on Kubernetes.

Installing the KubeRay operator

Follow the KubeRay quickstart guide to:

Install kubectl and Helm
Prepare a Kubernetes cluster
Deploy a KubeRay operator
Setting up a RayService custom resource (CR)

Once the KubeRay controller is running, manage your Ray Serve application by creating and updating a RayService CR (example).

Under the spec section in the RayService CR, set the following fields:

serveConfigV2: Represents the configuration that Ray Serve uses to deploy the application. Using serve build to print the Serve configuration and copy-paste it directly into your Kubernetes config and RayService CR.

rayClusterConfig: Populate this field with the contents of the spec field from the RayCluster CR YAML file. Refer to KubeRay configuration for more details.

Tip
To enhance the reliability of your application, particularly when dealing with large dependencies that may require a significant amount of time to download, consider including the dependencies in your image’s Dockerfile, so the dependencies are available as soon as the pods start.
Deploying a Serve application

When the RayService is created, the KubeRay controller first creates a Ray cluster using the provided configuration. Then, once the cluster is running, it deploys the Serve application to the cluster using the REST API. The controller also creates a Kubernetes Service that can be used to route traffic to the Serve application.

To see an example, deploy the Text ML example. The Serve config for the example is embedded into this sample RayService CR. Save this CR locally to a file named ray-service.text-ml.yaml:

Note
The example RayService uses very low numCpus values for demonstration purposes. In production, provide more resources to the Serve application. Learn more about how to configure KubeRay clusters here.
If you have dependencies that must be installed during deployment, you can add them to the runtime_env in the Deployment code. Learn more here
curl -o ray-service.text-ml.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ray-project/kuberay/2ba0dd7bea387ac9df3681666bab3d622e89846c/ray-operator/config/samples/ray-service.text-ml.yaml

To deploy the example, we simply kubectl apply the CR. This creates the underlying Ray cluster, consisting of a head and worker node pod (see Ray Clusters Key Concepts for more details on Ray clusters), as well as the service that can be used to query our application:

kubectl apply -f ray-service.text-ml.yaml

Perfect—let’s stand up a plain NGINX Ingress (no Helm chart), point it at the Ray Serve Service, and validate from outside the cluster.

## Actions taken

- Installed NGINX Ingress Controller (bare-metal manifest). The controller is up and registered IngressClass “nginx”.
- Created and applied a standalone Ingress that routes to your Serve Service:
  - backend: service `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc` port 8000
  - ingressClassName: nginx
  - added sane timeouts and body-size for embedding POSTs
- Verified end-to-end with nip.io host mapping:
  - Health: 200 OK via Ingress
  - Embeddings: success, shape [1, 384], processing_time ~11.6ms

I also added a reusable manifest in your repo at `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml` (with a CHANGE_ME host placeholder) so you can track/configure it in Git.

## How to reach it now

- Your cluster is using NodePort for the NGINX controller.
- Test from any machine that can reach your node IP:

Try it (replace <NODE_IP> with your node’s IP):

- HTTP with Host header (no DNS configured yet):
  - Health:
    - curl -H "Host: embeddings.<NODE_IP with dashes>.nip.io" http://<NODE_IP>:<nodePort>/health
  - Embeddings:
    - curl -H "Host: embeddings.<NODE_IP with dashes>.nip.io" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -X POST http://<NODE_IP>:<nodePort>/embeddings -d '{"texts":["hello"],"batch_size":32}'

Notes:
- The Ingress controller Service exposed ports: HTTP 80 on nodePort 30333, HTTPS 443 on 30278.
- Example host used here: embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io (nip.io maps that host back to 192.168.1.3 automatically).

## Customize the host

- Update `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml`:
  - Replace `embeddings.CHANGE_ME.nip.io` with your dashed IP (e.g., embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io) or your real domain.
  - Then apply it:
    - kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml

- If you have a real domain:
  - Create an A record pointing to the node IP (or, better, expose the Ingress via a LoadBalancer IP using MetalLB).
  - Update the host in the Ingress to your domain.

## Optional hardening (next)

- TLS: Install cert-manager and add:
  - annotation: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
  - spec.tls with your host and a secretName
- Auth: Add basic auth or mTLS at NGINX, or keep auth in FastAPI middleware.
- Rate limiting: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-* annotations.
- Ray dashboard: Use a separate Ingress to 8265 with restricted access (IP allowlist or auth).

## Files added

- `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml` — Standalone NGINX Ingress manifest pointing to `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000` with recommended annotations. Replace the host placeholder before applying for persistent configuration.

## Completion summary

- Ingress-NGINX installed and running.
- Ingress resource created and validated:
  - Health via Ingress: OK
  - Embeddings via Ingress: OK
- You can now access the service externally without in-cluster curl or port-forwarding.

{"filePath":"/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/docs/ingress-nginx.md","content":"# Standalone NGINX Ingress for EmbeddingService

This guide shows how to install a standalone NGINX Ingress Controller on Kubernetes and expose the Ray Serve HTTP service externally without port-forwarding. It includes tested commands, manifests, and request examples.

- Target backend: `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000` (ClusterIP)
- Objective: Reach the API from outside the cluster via `http(s)://<host>/...`


## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant N as NGINX Ingress Controller
    participant S as K8s Service (ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc)
    participant H as Ray Head (HTTP Proxy)
    participant W as Ray Worker Replica
    participant A as FastAPI App

    C->>N: HTTP POST /embeddings
    N->>S: Forward to ClusterIP:8000
    S->>H: Send to head (Serve HTTP proxy)
    H->>W: Route request to selected replica
    W->>A: Call FastAPI endpoint
    A-->>W: Return embedding vector(s)
    W-->>H: Response
    H-->>N: Response
    N-->>C: 200 OK (JSON)
```


## Prerequisites

- A working Kubernetes cluster (bare metal or cloud)
- KubeRay operator and your `RayService` deployed (so `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc` exists)
- kubectl access with cluster-admin permissions


## Option 1: Install NGINX Ingress (Bare Metal manifest)

This is the fastest path for single-node or bare-metal clusters.

```bash
# Install the controller (official manifest)
kubectl apply -f \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.11.1/deploy/static/provider/baremetal/deploy.yaml

# Wait for rollout
kubectl -n ingress-nginx rollout status deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --timeout=120s

# Confirm IngressClass is registered
kubectl get ingressclass

# Inspect the controller service (NodePort by default on bare metal)
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc -o wide
```

Expected output (example):

```
NAME                        TYPE       PORT(S)
ingress-nginx-controller    NodePort   80:30333/TCP,443:30278/TCP
```

If your cluster provides LoadBalancer (e.g., with MetalLB), you may see `EXTERNAL-IP` assigned. In that case, you won’t need NodePort.


## Option 2: Install via Helm (Alternative)

```bash
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update

# Basic install (may become LoadBalancer on cloud; NodePort on bare metal)
helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace
```

You can set a specific Service type with Helm values if needed:

```bash
helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort
```


## Ingress resource (HTTP)

Create an Ingress that points to the Ray Serve service (`ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000`). You can use a DNS name or a nip.io host that maps back to your node IP.

- A copy lives in the repo at `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml`.
- Replace `CHANGE_ME` with your dashed IP or domain.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: embedding-service-ingress
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "300"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "300"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: embeddings.CHANGE_ME.nip.io   # e.g., embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc
            port:
              number: 8000
```

Apply it:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml
kubectl get ingress embedding-service-ingress -o wide
```


## Quick test with nip.io

Define convenience variables for testing:

```bash
# Node IP of the machine running the cluster
export NODE_IP=$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}')
# NodePort of HTTP (80) on the ingress controller
export NODE_PORT=$(kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc ingress-nginx-controller \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[?(@.port==80)].nodePort}')
# Transform 192.168.1.3 -> 192-168-1-3
export HOST_DASH=${NODE_IP//./-}
export HOST="embeddings.${HOST_DASH}.nip.io"
# Single endpoint string (handy for scripts)
export ENDPOINT="http://${HOST}:${NODE_PORT}"

echo NODE_IP=$NODE_IP
echo NODE_PORT=$NODE_PORT
echo HOST=$HOST
echo ENDPOINT=$ENDPOINT
```

Sanity-check the API through the Ingress:

```bash

curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health | jq .

# Embeddings
curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -X POST $ENDPOINT/embeddings \
  -d '{"texts":["hello from ingress"],"batch_size":32}' | jq '{shape,processing_time}'

# Stats
curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/embeddings/stats | jq '{semaphore_status, gpu_stats}'
```

If you configured a real domain and DNS, you won’t need the Host header. Just call `http(s)://your.domain/...` directly.


## Optional: HTTPS with cert-manager

To enable TLS with Let’s Encrypt:

1) Install cert-manager

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.15.3/cert-manager.yaml
```

2) Create a ClusterIssuer (Let’s Encrypt)

```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: you@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          class: nginx
```

3) Update the Ingress

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - embeddings.example.com
    secretName: embeddings-tls
```

Re-apply the Ingress and wait for the certificate to be issued.


## Production recommendations

- Timeouts & body sizes: tune via NGINX annotations based on typical request sizes and latency
- Security: consider IP allowlists, WAF, mTLS, or auth at the edge; always validate in FastAPI
- Observability: enable NGINX access logs and Prometheus metrics; scrape your app `/metrics`
- Ray dashboard: expose separately (different host) and restrict access
- LoadBalancer: on bare metal, pair with MetalLB for a stable external IP


## Troubleshooting

- 404 Not Found:
  - Host header doesn’t match the Ingress host
  - Wrong path or missing pathType: Prefix
- 502/504 Gateway:
  - Service/pods not ready; check `kubectl get pods` and app logs
  - Increase `proxy-read-timeout`/`proxy-send-timeout`
- 413 Request Entity Too Large:
  - Increase `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size`
- Can’t reach NodePort:
  - Firewalls (UFW/iptables) may block the NodePort; allow traffic
  - On multi-node clusters, target the node where the controller is running or expose via LoadBalancer


## Reference

- `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml` in this repo (ready-to-use template)
- NGINX Ingress Controller docs: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/
- KubeRay + Ray Serve on K8s docs: https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/production-guide/kubernetes.html

# Standalone NGINX Ingress for EmbeddingService

This guide shows how to install a standalone NGINX Ingress Controller on Kubernetes and expose the Ray Serve HTTP service externally without port-forwarding. It includes tested commands, manifests, and request examples.

- Target backend: `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000` (ClusterIP)
- Objective: Reach the API from outside the cluster via `http(s)://<host>/...`

Who is this for
- Teams running KubeRay/RayService that want a stable, external HTTP endpoint
- Bare-metal or single-node K8s users who don’t have a cloud LoadBalancer

What you’ll get
- A running NGINX Ingress Controller
- An Ingress resource pointing to your Serve Service
- Copy-pasteable curl examples that work immediately (using nip.io)

Success criteria
- External curl to `/health` returns JSON with `{ "status": "healthy" }`
- POST to `/embeddings` returns an embedding shape and processing time


## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant N as NGINX Ingress Controller
    participant S as K8s Service (ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc)
    participant H as Ray Head (HTTP Proxy)
    participant W as Ray Worker Replica
    participant A as FastAPI App

    C->>N: HTTP POST /embeddings
    N->>S: Forward to ClusterIP:8000
    S->>H: Send to head (Serve HTTP proxy)
    H->>W: Route request to selected replica
    W->>A: Call FastAPI endpoint
    A-->>W: Return embedding vector(s)
    W-->>H: Response
    H-->>N: Response
    N-->>C: 200 OK (JSON)
```

Explanation
- The Ingress Controller terminates HTTP(S) at the cluster edge and routes based on Host/Path to the correct K8s Service.
- KubeRay creates a dedicated ClusterIP service for Ray Serve HTTP: `*-serve-svc` (port 8000). Point your Ingress to this service.
- The head node runs the Serve HTTP proxy; it routes your request to an appropriate worker replica where your FastAPI app executes.
- For the Ray dashboard (8265), use a separate, restricted Ingress that targets the head service; keep it isolated from the API.


## Prerequisites

- A working Kubernetes cluster (bare metal or cloud)
- KubeRay operator and your `RayService` deployed (so `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc` exists)
- kubectl access with cluster-admin permissions

Helpful checks
- Namespace: examples here use `default`. Adjust if you deployed into another namespace.
- Verify service: `kubectl get svc ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc -o wide`
- Pods ready: `kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=<your-cluster>`


## Option 1: Install NGINX Ingress (Bare Metal manifest)

This is the fastest path for single-node or bare-metal clusters.

```bash
# Install the controller (official manifest)
kubectl apply -f \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.11.1/deploy/static/provider/baremetal/deploy.yaml

# Wait for rollout
kubectl -n ingress-nginx rollout status deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --timeout=120s

# Confirm IngressClass is registered
kubectl get ingressclass

# Inspect the controller service (NodePort by default on bare metal)
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc -o wide
```

Expected output (example):

```
NAME                        TYPE       PORT(S)
ingress-nginx-controller    NodePort   80:30333/TCP,443:30278/TCP
```

If your cluster provides LoadBalancer (e.g., with MetalLB), you may see `EXTERNAL-IP` assigned. In that case, you won’t need NodePort.

Choose this if
- You’re on bare metal or kind/minikube without a managed LoadBalancer
- You want the simplest possible setup with minimal dependencies

What this creates
- Namespace `ingress-nginx`
- Deployment `ingress-nginx-controller`
- Service `ingress-nginx-controller` (NodePort by default)
- IngressClass `nginx`

Security note
- NodePort opens a high TCP port on cluster nodes; ensure your firewall allows only the sources you expect.


## Option 2: Install via Helm (Alternative)

```bash
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update

# Basic install (may become LoadBalancer on cloud; NodePort on bare metal)
helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace
```

You can set a specific Service type with Helm values if needed:
Choose this if
- You prefer Helm lifecycle management and easier upgrades/values overrides
- You’re on cloud K8s and want `LoadBalancer` with an external IP

```bash
helm upgrade --install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.type=NodePort
```


## Ingress resource (HTTP)

Create an Ingress that points to the Ray Serve service (`ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000`). You can use a DNS name or a nip.io host that maps back to your node IP.

- A copy lives in the repo at `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml`.
- Replace `CHANGE_ME` with your dashed IP or domain.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: embedding-service-ingress
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "300"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "300"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: embeddings.CHANGE_ME.nip.io   # e.g., embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc
            port:
              number: 8000
```

Apply it:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml
kubectl get ingress embedding-service-ingress -o wide
```


## Quick test with nip.io

Define convenience variables for testing:

```bash
# Node IP of the machine running the cluster
export NODE_IP=$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}')
# NodePort of HTTP (80) on the ingress controller
export NODE_PORT=$(kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc ingress-nginx-controller \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[?(@.port==80)].nodePort}')
# Transform 192.168.1.3 -> 192-168-1-3
export HOST_DASH=${NODE_IP//./-}
export HOST="embeddings.${HOST_DASH}.nip.io"
# Single endpoint string (handy for scripts)
export ENDPOINT="http://${HOST}:${NODE_PORT}"

echo NODE_IP=$NODE_IP
echo NODE_PORT=$NODE_PORT
echo HOST=$HOST
echo ENDPOINT=$ENDPOINT
```

Sanity-check the API through the Ingress:

```bash
# Health
curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health | jq .

# Embeddings
curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -X POST $ENDPOINT/embeddings \
  -d '{"texts":["hello from ingress"],"batch_size":32}' | jq '{shape,processing_time}'

# Stats
curl -sS -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/embeddings/stats | jq '{semaphore_status, gpu_stats}'
```

If you configured a real domain and DNS, you won’t need the Host header. Just call `http(s)://your.domain/...` directly.

Expected outputs
- Health: `{ "status": "healthy", "timestamp": "..." }`
- Embeddings: `{ "shape": [N, 384], "processing_time": <seconds> }`
- Stats: shows semaphore availability and GPU info; useful to confirm the request truly hit your app through the Ingress path.

When to use nip.io vs. DNS
- nip.io is perfect for quick tests on bare metal—no DNS change required
- For production, create an A record pointing to your Ingress external IP (or node IP/MetalLB VIP)


## Optional: HTTPS with cert-manager

To enable TLS with Let’s Encrypt:

1) Install cert-manager

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.15.3/cert-manager.yaml
```

2) Create a ClusterIssuer (Let’s Encrypt)

```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: you@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          class: nginx
```

3) Update the Ingress

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - embeddings.example.com
    secretName: embeddings-tls
```

Re-apply the Ingress and wait for the certificate to be issued.

Tip: start with Let’s Encrypt staging to avoid rate limits
```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: you@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging
    solvers:
    - http01:
        ingress:
          class: nginx
```
Once verified, switch the Ingress annotation to `letsencrypt-prod`.


## Production recommendations

- Timeouts & body sizes: tune via NGINX annotations based on typical request sizes and latency
- Security: consider IP allowlists, WAF, mTLS, or auth at the edge; always validate in FastAPI
- Observability: enable NGINX access logs and Prometheus metrics; scrape your app `/metrics`
- Ray dashboard: expose separately (different host) and restrict access
- LoadBalancer: on bare metal, pair with MetalLB for a stable external IP

Forwarded headers
- NGINX adds `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` by default
- Your app can read these to log client IPs correctly (this repo already checks `X-Real-IP`)

CORS
- Prefer handling CORS in FastAPI for clarity and testability
- If you need to enforce at the edge, use NGINX annotations or a snippet to set CORS headers


## Troubleshooting

- 404 Not Found:
  - Host header doesn’t match the Ingress host
  - Wrong path or missing pathType: Prefix
- 502/504 Gateway:
  - Service/pods not ready; check `kubectl get pods` and app logs
  - Increase `proxy-read-timeout`/`proxy-send-timeout`
- 413 Request Entity Too Large:
  - Increase `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size`
- Can’t reach NodePort:
  - Firewalls (UFW/iptables) may block the NodePort; allow traffic
  - On multi-node clusters, target the node where the controller is running or expose via LoadBalancer

Deep dive commands
- Describe resources for events:
  - `kubectl describe ingress embedding-service-ingress`
  - `kubectl -n ingress-nginx describe svc ingress-nginx-controller`
- Controller logs (filter by host):
  - `kubectl -n ingress-nginx logs deploy/ingress-nginx-controller -f | grep embeddings`
- Verify Service endpoints:
  - `kubectl get endpoints ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc -o wide`
- Test in-cluster path end-to-end:
  - `kubectl run -it tmp --rm --image=curlimages/curl -- sh`
  - `curl -s http://ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000/health`
- Host/network
  - Ensure `NODE_PORT` is open on your firewall, e.g., `sudo ufw allow 30333/tcp`

FAQ
- Why not point Ingress to the head service? The `*-serve-svc` is the dedicated HTTP entry for Ray Serve (port 8000). The head service bundles multiple ports and is better reserved for internal cluster comms and the dashboard.
- How do I expose the dashboard? Create a separate Ingress routing to port 8265 on the head service, and restrict access with auth/IP allowlists.
- Can I use a path prefix (e.g., `/api`)? Yes—set the Ingress path to `/api` and ensure your app routes match. If you need to rewrite paths, add an appropriate NGINX rewrite annotation.


## Reference

- `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml` in this repo (ready-to-use template)
- NGINX Ingress Controller docs: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/
- KubeRay + Ray Serve on K8s docs: https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/production-guide/kubernetes.html

+- Teams running KubeRay/RayService that want a stable, external HTTP endpoint
+- Bare-metal or single-node K8s users who don’t have a cloud LoadBalancer
+
+What you’ll get
+- A running NGINX Ingress Controller
+- An Ingress resource pointing to your Serve Service
+- Copy-pasteable curl examples that work immediately (using nip.io)
+
+Success criteria
+- External curl to `/health` returns JSON with `{ "status": "healthy" }`
+- POST to `/embeddings` returns an embedding shape and processing time
@@
 ## Architecture
@@
 ```mermaid
@@
 ```
+
+Explanation
+- The Ingress Controller terminates HTTP(S) at the cluster edge and routes based on Host/Path to the correct K8s Service.
+- KubeRay creates a dedicated ClusterIP service for Ray Serve HTTP: `*-serve-svc` (port 8000). Point your Ingress to this service.
+- The head node runs the Serve HTTP proxy; it routes your request to an appropriate worker replica where your FastAPI app executes.
+- For the Ray dashboard (8265), use a separate, restricted Ingress that targets the head service; keep it isolated from the API.
@@
 ## Prerequisites
 
 - A working Kubernetes cluster (bare metal or cloud)
 - KubeRay operator and your `RayService` deployed (so `ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc` exists)
 - kubectl access with cluster-admin permissions
+
+Helpful checks
+- Namespace: examples here use `default`. Adjust if you deployed into another namespace.
+- Verify service: `kubectl get svc ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc -o wide`
+- Pods ready: `kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=<your-cluster>`
@@
 ## Option 1: Install NGINX Ingress (Bare Metal manifest)
 
 This is the fastest path for single-node or bare-metal clusters.
@@
 Expected output (example):
@@
 If your cluster provides LoadBalancer (e.g., with MetalLB), you may see `EXTERNAL-IP` assigned. In that case, you won’t need NodePort.
+
+Choose this if
+- You’re on bare metal or kind/minikube without a managed LoadBalancer
+- You want the simplest possible setup with minimal dependencies
+
+What this creates
+- Namespace `ingress-nginx`
+- Deployment `ingress-nginx-controller`
+- Service `ingress-nginx-controller` (NodePort by default)
+- IngressClass `nginx`
+
+Security note
+- NodePort opens a high TCP port on cluster nodes; ensure your firewall allows only the sources you expect.
@@
 ## Option 2: Install via Helm (Alternative)
@@
 You can set a specific Service type with Helm values if needed:
@@
+Choose this if
+- You prefer Helm lifecycle management and easier upgrades/values overrides
+- You’re on cloud K8s and want `LoadBalancer` with an external IP
@@
 ## Ingress resource (HTTP)
@@
 - A copy lives in the repo at `k8s/ingress-nginx.yaml`.
 - Replace `CHANGE_ME` with your dashed IP or domain.
@@
 Apply it:
@@
 
 
 ## Quick test with nip.io
 
 Define convenience variables for testing:
@@
 Sanity-check the API through the Ingress:
@@
 If you configured a real domain and DNS, you won’t need the Host header. Just call `http(s)://your.domain/...` directly.
+
+Expected outputs
+- Health: `{ "status": "healthy", "timestamp": "..." }`
+- Embeddings: `{ "shape": [N, 384], "processing_time": <seconds> }`
+- Stats: shows semaphore availability and GPU info; useful to confirm the request truly hit your app through the Ingress path.
+
+When to use nip.io vs. DNS
+- nip.io is perfect for quick tests on bare metal—no DNS change required
+- For production, create an A record pointing to your Ingress external IP (or node IP/MetalLB VIP)
@@
 ## Optional: HTTPS with cert-manager
@@
 2) Create a ClusterIssuer (Let’s Encrypt)
@@
 3) Update the Ingress
@@
 Re-apply the Ingress and wait for the certificate to be issued.
+
+Tip: start with Let’s Encrypt staging to avoid rate limits
+```yaml
+apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
+kind: ClusterIssuer
+metadata:
+  name: letsencrypt-staging
+spec:
+  acme:
+    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
+    email: you@example.com
+    privateKeySecretRef:
+      name: letsencrypt-staging
+    solvers:
+    - http01:
+        ingress:
+          class: nginx
+```
+Once verified, switch the Ingress annotation to `letsencrypt-prod`.
@@
 ## Production recommendations
@@
 - Timeouts & body sizes: tune via NGINX annotations based on typical request sizes and latency
 - Security: consider IP allowlists, WAF, mTLS, or auth at the edge; always validate in FastAPI
 - Observability: enable NGINX access logs and Prometheus metrics; scrape your app `/metrics`
 - Ray dashboard: expose separately (different host) and restrict access
 - LoadBalancer: on bare metal, pair with MetalLB for a stable external IP
+
+Forwarded headers
+- NGINX adds `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` by default
+- Your app can read these to log client IPs correctly (this repo already checks `X-Real-IP`)
+
+CORS
+- Prefer handling CORS in FastAPI for clarity and testability
+- If you need to enforce at the edge, use NGINX annotations or a snippet to set CORS headers
@@
 ## Troubleshooting
@@
 - 404 Not Found:
   - Host header doesn’t match the Ingress host
   - Wrong path or missing pathType: Prefix
 - 502/504 Gateway:
   - Service/pods not ready; check `kubectl get pods` and app logs
   - Increase `proxy-read-timeout`/`proxy-send-timeout`
 - 413 Request Entity Too Large:
   - Increase `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size`
 - Can’t reach NodePort:
   - Firewalls (UFW/iptables) may block the NodePort; allow traffic
   - On multi-node clusters, target the node where the controller is running or expose via LoadBalancer
+
+Deep dive commands
+- Describe resources for events:
+  - `kubectl describe ingress embedding-service-ingress`
+  - `kubectl -n ingress-nginx describe svc ingress-nginx-controller`
+- Controller logs (filter by host):
+  - `kubectl -n ingress-nginx logs deploy/ingress-nginx-controller -f | grep embeddings`
+- Verify Service endpoints:
+  - `kubectl get endpoints ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc -o wide`
+- Test in-cluster path end-to-end:
+  - `kubectl run -it tmp --rm --image=curlimages/curl -- sh`
+  - `curl -s http://ray-cluster-simple-serve-svc:8000/health`
+- Host/network
+  - Ensure `NODE_PORT` is open on your firewall, e.g., `sudo ufw allow 30333/tcp`
+
+FAQ
+- Why not point Ingress to the head service? The `*-serve-svc` is the dedicated HTTP entry for Ray Serve (port 8000). The head service bundles multiple ports and is better reserved for internal cluster comms and the dashboard.
+- How do I expose the dashboard? Create a separate Ingress routing to port 8265 on the head service, and restrict access with auth/IP allowlists.
+- Can I use a path prefix (e.g., `/api`)? Yes—set the Ingress path to `/api` and ensure your app routes match. If you need to rewrite paths, add an appropriate NGINX rewrite annotation.
@@

"""
Ray Serve deployment wrapper for EmbeddingService.

This module wraps the existing FastAPI application with Ray Serve
decorators to enable distributed deployment with autoscaling and
load balancing. No changes to the existing application logic required.
"""

from ray import serve

# Import the existing FastAPI app
from src.service.main import app


@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,  # Allow 2 replicas per GPU
    },
    # Increase per-replica concurrency to avoid quick 500s under short bursts.
    # Default is 5; raising this increases the number of in-flight requests a replica will accept
    # before the Serve proxy rejects. Tune based on model latency and resource headroom.
    max_ongoing_requests=20,
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    """
    Ray Serve deployment that wraps the FastAPI application.
    
    The @serve.ingress decorator makes all FastAPI routes available
    through Ray Serve, preserving all existing endpoints, middleware,
    and business logic without modification.
    """
    pass


# Deployment binding for Ray Serve
deployment = EmbeddingServiceDeployment.bind()

- Adjust autoscaling sensitivity
  - Increase `target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica` to 6–8 for more aggressive scale-up (trade-off: more concurrent work per replica).

- Ingress retries (quick client-facing mitigation)
  - At NGINX, enable limited retries on 500 to smooth short spikes:
    - `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream: "error timeout http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504"`
    - `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream-tries: "2"`
  - Note: POST retries are generally “unsafe,” but for idempotent embeddings with the same body it’s typically acceptable.

- Prefer 429 instead of 500
  - Ray Serve emits 500 on overload rejection. If you want clients to back off explicitly, we can front this with a small proxy (or adjust NGINX to map known “over capacity” responses to 429 with `Retry-After`)—more work, but clearer semantics.

## What we learned from the logs

- Serve proxy confirms 500s are coming from the backend under load, not ingress timeouts.
- Replica logs show “max_ongoing_requests=5” capacity exceeded warnings exactly during the burst, explaining the 500s.
- No app-level exceptions or stack traces around those times—this is purely capacity behavior.

## Next steps

- Redeploy with the updated `max_ongoing_requests=20`.
- Re-run your 50× burst and share the new distribution; we should see 200s across the board and similar latency, possibly slightly higher p95 due to concurrency.
- If needed, we’ll tune min replicas and/or autoscaling target for your real peak traffic profile.

# Forceful Redeploy

## Quick Ray Cluster Forced Redeployment Process

### 1. Delete Current Deployment
```bash
kubectl delete raycluster ray-cluster-simple
```

### 2. Force Delete Stuck Pods (if needed)
```bash
# Check for terminating pods
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple

# Force delete if stuck in Terminating state
kubectl delete pod ray-cluster-simple-head-* ray-cluster-simple-worker-* --force --grace-period=0
```

### 3. Verify Clean State
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
# Should return "No resources found"
```

### 4. Redeploy with Updated Configuration
```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
```

### 5. Monitor New Deployment
```bash
# Watch pod creation
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w

# Check specific pod status
kubectl describe pod ray-cluster-simple-head-<pod-id>
```

### 6. Quick Health Check
```bash
# Wait for pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s

# Verify all containers running
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
```

### Expected Results
- **Head pod**: 2/2 Ready (ray-head + autoscaler containers)
- **Worker pods**: 1/1 Ready (ray-worker containers)  
- **No CrashLoopBackOff** if rayStartParams properly configured

### Troubleshooting
If pods still crash after redeploy:
1. Check autoscaler logs: `kubectl logs <head-pod> -c autoscaler`
2. Verify rayStartParams in YAML configuration
3. Check image pull issues: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`

edits.text:
# Service Update & Deployment Guide

This guide walks you through rolling out a code/config change to the Embedding Service on Ray/Kubernetes, validating the rollout, and monitoring for regressions. It includes runnable command snippets and a couple of Mermaid sequence/flow diagrams for the big picture.

Links to related docs:
- `docs/headnode-log-discovery.md` — where to find Ray logs on head/worker nodes
- `docs/forceful-redeploy.md` — force a clean redeploy if needed
- `docs/ingress-nginx.md` — exposing the service externally via NGINX Ingress

---

## What changed (example)

In this rollout, we increased the per-replica concurrency to absorb ingress bursts without 500s from Serve overload rejections.

File: `src/service/ray_deployment.py`

```python
@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,
    },
    # Raised from default (5) to 20 to reduce overload 500s during bursts
    max_ongoing_requests=20,
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    pass
```

You can adapt these values to your traffic profile and resource budget.

---

## High-level rollout path

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Reg as Docker Registry
    participant K8s as K8s + KubeRay
    participant RS as RayService
    participant Pods as Ray Head/Workers
    participant Ing as NGINX Ingress
    participant Cl as Clients

    Dev->>Dev: Edit code/config
    Dev->>Reg: docker build && push new tag
    Dev->>K8s: kubectl apply -f RayService (new tag)
    K8s->>RS: Reconcile
    RS->>Pods: Create/Update head + workers + Serve app
    Cl-->>Ing: Send requests
    Ing-->>Pods: Forward to Serve proxy/replicas
    Pods-->>Cl: Responses
```

---

## Prerequisites

- kubectl context points to the right cluster/namespace (RayService lives in `default` by default)
- Access to your container registry (example below uses a local registry: `192.168.1.3:5000`)
- The RayService manifest at `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml`

---

## Step 1 — Build and push the image

Update the image tag as needed. Example uses `ray-latest-v2`.

```bash
docker build -t 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2 .
docker push 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2
```

If you version with a file (like `version`), bump it before the build.

---

## Step 2 — Point the RayService to the new image

Confirm your RayService uses the updated image (both head and workers). Example: `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml` (snippet):

```yaml
spec:
  rayClusterConfig:
    headGroupSpec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: "192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2"
            imagePullPolicy: Always
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: worker-gpu
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2
            imagePullPolicy: Always
```

Apply the manifest:

```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl get rayservice -A -o wide
```

Note: A simple `apply` often triggers a rolling update. If ports/GPU reservations are stuck on the node, use a forceful redeploy (next section).

---

## Step 3 — Forceful redeploy (when in doubt)

If you see pods Pending due to hostPort collisions or GPU scheduling, follow `docs/forceful-redeploy.md`. Quick reference:

```bash
# Remove existing RayService (operator will clean up the cluster)
kubectl delete rayservice ray-cluster-simple --wait=true

# If any pods linger in Terminating, force delete them
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
kubectl delete pod <old-pod-names> --force --grace-period=0

# Recreate
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml

# Watch
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
```

Common Pending cause: “didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports” — resolve by ensuring old head/worker pods are fully removed (force delete if necessary).

---

## Step 4 — Wait for readiness

```bash
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -o wide
```

You should see the head pod Running with the expected ports and the worker pods Running (GPU ready if applicable).

---

## Step 5 — Quick health checks (via Ingress)

Set convenience variables to test through NGINX Ingress and nip.io (adapt to your env):

```bash
export NODE_IP=<your-node-ip>                 # e.g., 192.168.1.3
export NODE_PORT=<ingress-nodeport-http>      # e.g., 30333
export HOST=embeddings.${NODE_IP//./-}.nip.io
export ENDPOINT=http://$HOST:$NODE_PORT

curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health | jq .
curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"texts":["hello ingress"],"batch_size":32}' \
  $ENDPOINT/embeddings | jq .
```

---

## Step 6 — Burst test and summarize

Run a small burst (50 req, P=10) and summarize status codes and latency:

```bash
seq 50 | xargs -n1 -P 10 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code},%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"texts":["hello world"]}' $ENDPOINT/embeddings | tee /tmp/burst.csv

awk -F, '{counts[$1]++} END{for (c in counts) printf("%s %d\n", c, counts[c])}' /tmp/burst.csv | sort
awk -F, '{sum+=$2; n++} END{printf("mean=%.4fs n=%d\n", sum/n, n)}' /tmp/burst.csv
cut -d, -f2 /tmp/burst.csv | sort -n | awk 'BEGIN{p50n=0;p95n=0} {vals[NR]=$1} END{n=NR;p50i=int(0.5*n); if(p50i<1)p50i=1; p95i=int(0.95*n); if(p95i<1)p95i=1; printf("p50=%.4fs p95=%.4fs count=%d\n", vals[p50i], vals[p95i], n)}'
```

Expected after the concurrency tweak: 200s across the board for this small burst; p50 ~20–40ms depending on model size and hardware.

---

## Step 7 — Monitor Ray logs (head + replicas)

See `docs/headnode-log-discovery.md` for more. Handy snippets:

```bash
HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# Serve proxy on the head
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log

# Per-replica logs on workers
for W in $(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=worker -o name); do
  kubectl exec ${W#pod/} -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_ || true
done

# Look for overload messages or exceptions
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- sh -lc "grep -RniE 'ERROR|Exception|Traceback|capacity' /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs | tail -n 200"
```

If you previously saw fast 500s during bursts, look for lines like:

```
WARNING replica.py:571 - Replica at capacity of max_ongoing_requests=5, rejecting request ...
```

After raising `max_ongoing_requests`, these should go away for the same burst level.

---

## Optional — Ingress retry & timeouts

You can smooth out brief backend hiccups by allowing limited retries at the ingress. Example annotations for your `Ingress` manifest:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "120"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream: "error timeout http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream-tries: "2"
```

Note: Retries on POST are generally “unsafe.” For idempotent embeddings this is typically acceptable—but validate with your product requirements.

---

## Rollback

If performance or error rates regress, roll back by pointing the RayService back to the previous image tag and re-apply. If pods hang on ports/GPUs, use the forceful redeploy steps.

```bash
# revert image tag in ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
```

---

## Troubleshooting flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Apply new image/tag] --> B{Pods Pending?}
    B -- No --> C[Wait for Ready & test]
    B -- Yes --> D[Check Events: hostPort/GPU]
    D -->|hostPort in use| E[Force delete old pods]
    D -->|GPU not free| F[Drain/adjust resources]
    E --> G[Re-apply RayService]
    F --> G
    C --> H{Burst 500s?}
    H -- No --> I[Done]
    H -- Yes --> J[Check Serve logs for capacity]
    J -->|capacity rejects| K[Raise max_ongoing_requests or add replicas]
    J -->|exceptions| L[Fix app errors]
    K --> C
    L --> C
```

---

## Acceptance checklist

- RayService is Running; head/worker pods are Ready
- Health endpoint returns 200 via ingress
- Embeddings endpoint returns 200 for single request
- Burst test shows 0% 500s at your target concurrency (baseline P=10)
- No new warnings/errors in Serve proxy/replica logs

---

## Appendix — Frequently used commands

```bash
# Describe a problematic pod
kubectl describe pod <pod>

# Tail Serve controller/proxy logs on head
HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/controller_*.log
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log

# List per-replica logs on a worker
WORKER=<worker-pod>
kubectl exec $WORKER -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_

# Quick ingress health
curl -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health
```

+Confirm your RayService uses the updated image (both head and workers). Example: `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml` (snippet):
+
+```yaml
+spec:
+  rayClusterConfig:
+    headGroupSpec:
+      template:
+        spec:
+          containers:
+          - name: ray-head
+            image: "192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2"
+            imagePullPolicy: Always
+    workerGroupSpecs:
+    - groupName: worker-gpu
+      template:
+        spec:
+          containers:
+          - name: ray-worker
+            image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2
+            imagePullPolicy: Always
+```
+
+Apply the manifest:
+
+```bash
+kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
+kubectl get rayservice -A -o wide
+```
+
+Note: A simple `apply` often triggers a rolling update. If ports/GPU reservations are stuck on the node, use a forceful redeploy (next section).
+
+---
+
+## Step 3 — Forceful redeploy (when in doubt)
+
+If you see pods Pending due to hostPort collisions or GPU scheduling, follow `docs/forceful-redeploy.md`. Quick reference:
+
+```bash
+# Remove existing RayService (operator will clean up the cluster)
+kubectl delete rayservice ray-cluster-simple --wait=true
+
+# If any pods linger in Terminating, force delete them
+kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
+kubectl delete pod <old-pod-names> --force --grace-period=0
+
+# Recreate
+kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
+
+# Watch
+kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
+```
+
+Common Pending cause: “didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports” — resolve by ensuring old head/worker pods are fully removed (force delete if necessary).
+
+---
+
+## Step 4 — Wait for readiness
+
+```bash
+kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s
+kubectl get pods -o wide
+```
+
+You should see the head pod Running with the expected ports and the worker pods Running (GPU ready if applicable).
+
+---
+
+## Step 5 — Quick health checks (via Ingress)
+
+Set convenience variables to test through NGINX Ingress and nip.io (adapt to your env):
+
+```bash
+export NODE_IP=<your-node-ip>                 # e.g., 192.168.1.3
+export NODE_PORT=<ingress-nodeport-http>      # e.g., 30333
+export HOST=embeddings.${NODE_IP//./-}.nip.io
+export ENDPOINT=http://$HOST:$NODE_PORT
+
+curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health | jq .
+curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+  -d '{"texts":["hello ingress"],"batch_size":32}' \
+  $ENDPOINT/embeddings | jq .
+```
+
+---
+
+## Step 6 — Burst test and summarize
+
+Run a small burst (50 req, P=10) and summarize status codes and latency:
+
+```bash
+seq 50 | xargs -n1 -P 10 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code},%{time_total}\n' \
+  -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
+  -d '{"texts":["hello world"]}' $ENDPOINT/embeddings | tee /tmp/burst.csv
+
+awk -F, '{counts[$1]++} END{for (c in counts) printf("%s %d\n", c, counts[c])}' /tmp/burst.csv | sort
+awk -F, '{sum+=$2; n++} END{printf("mean=%.4fs n=%d\n", sum/n, n)}' /tmp/burst.csv
+cut -d, -f2 /tmp/burst.csv | sort -n | awk 'BEGIN{p50n=0;p95n=0} {vals[NR]=$1} END{n=NR;p50i=int(0.5*n); if(p50i<1)p50i=1; p95i=int(0.95*n); if(p95i<1)p95i=1; printf("p50=%.4fs p95=%.4fs count=%d\n", vals[p50i], vals[p95i], n)}'
+```
+
+Expected after the concurrency tweak: 200s across the board for this small burst; p50 ~20–40ms depending on model size and hardware.
+
+---
+
+## Step 7 — Monitor Ray logs (head + replicas)
+
+See `docs/headnode-log-discovery.md` for more. Handy snippets:
+
+```bash
+HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
+
+# Serve proxy on the head
+kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log
+
+# Per-replica logs on workers
+for W in $(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=worker -o name); do
+  kubectl exec ${W#pod/} -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_ || true
+done
+
+# Look for overload messages or exceptions
+kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- sh -lc "grep -RniE 'ERROR|Exception|Traceback|capacity' /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs | tail -n 200"
+```
+
+If you previously saw fast 500s during bursts, look for lines like:
+
+```
+WARNING replica.py:571 - Replica at capacity of max_ongoing_requests=5, rejecting request ...
+```
+
+After raising `max_ongoing_requests`, these should go away for the same burst level.
+
+---
+
+## Optional — Ingress retry & timeouts
+
+You can smooth out brief backend hiccups by allowing limited retries at the ingress. Example annotations for your `Ingress` manifest:
+
+```yaml
+metadata:
+  annotations:
+    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
+    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120"
+    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "120"
+    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream: "error timeout http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504"
+    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream-tries: "2"
+```
+
+Note: Retries on POST are generally “unsafe.” For idempotent embeddings this is typically acceptable—but validate with your product requirements.
+
+---
+
+## Rollback
+
+If performance or error rates regress, roll back by pointing the RayService back to the previous image tag and re-apply. If pods hang on ports/GPUs, use the forceful redeploy steps.
+
+```bash
+# revert image tag in ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
+kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
+kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
+```
+
+---
+
+## Troubleshooting flow
+
+```mermaid
+flowchart TD
+    A[Apply new image/tag] --> B{Pods Pending?}
+    B -- No --> C[Wait for Ready & test]
+    B -- Yes --> D[Check Events: hostPort/GPU]
+    D -->|hostPort in use| E[Force delete old pods]
+    D -->|GPU not free| F[Drain/adjust resources]
+    E --> G[Re-apply RayService]
+    F --> G
+    C --> H{Burst 500s?}
+    H -- No --> I[Done]
+    H -- Yes --> J[Check Serve logs for capacity]
+    J -->|capacity rejects| K[Raise max_ongoing_requests or add replicas]
+    J -->|exceptions| L[Fix app errors]
+    K --> C
+    L --> C
+```
+
+---
+
+## Acceptance checklist
+
+- RayService is Running; head/worker pods are Ready
+- Health endpoint returns 200 via ingress
+- Embeddings endpoint returns 200 for single request
+- Burst test shows 0% 500s at your target concurrency (baseline P=10)
+- No new warnings/errors in Serve proxy/replica logs
+
+---
+
+## Appendix — Frequently used commands
+
+```bash
+# Describe a problematic pod
+kubectl describe pod <pod>
+
+# Tail Serve controller/proxy logs on head
+HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
+kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/controller_*.log
+kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log
+
+# List per-replica logs on a worker
+WORKER=<worker-pod>
+kubectl exec $WORKER -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_
+
+# Quick ingress health
+curl -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health
+```
+
*** End Patch","explanation":"Add a comprehensive rollout guide with steps, commands, and Mermaid diagrams to deploy the updated service, validate via ingress, monitor logs, and troubleshoot pending pods or 500s."}

"""
Ray Serve deployment wrapper for EmbeddingService.

This module wraps the existing FastAPI application with Ray Serve
decorators to enable distributed deployment with autoscaling and
load balancing. No changes to the existing application logic required.
"""

from ray import serve

# Import the existing FastAPI app
from src.service.main import app


@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,  # Allow 2 replicas per GPU
    },
    # Increase per-replica concurrency to avoid quick 500s under short bursts.
    # Default is 5; raising this increases the number of in-flight requests a replica will accept
    # before the Serve proxy rejects. Tune based on model latency and resource headroom.
        max_ongoing_requests=64,
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    """
    Ray Serve deployment that wraps the FastAPI application.
    
    The @serve.ingress decorator makes all FastAPI routes available
    through Ray Serve, preserving all existing endpoints, middleware,
    and business logic without modification.
    """
    pass


# Deployment binding for Ray Serve
deployment = EmbeddingServiceDeployment.bind()

# Forceful Redeploy

## Quick Ray Cluster Forced Redeployment Process

### 1. Delete Current Deployment
```bash
kubectl delete raycluster ray-cluster-simple
```

### 2. Force Delete Stuck Pods (if needed)
```bash
# Check for terminating pods
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple

# Force delete if stuck in Terminating state
kubectl delete pod ray-cluster-simple-head-* ray-cluster-simple-worker-* --force --grace-period=0
```

### 3. Verify Clean State
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
# Should return "No resources found"
```

### 4. Redeploy with Updated Configuration
```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
```

### 5. Monitor New Deployment
```bash
# Watch pod creation
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w

# Check specific pod status
kubectl describe pod ray-cluster-simple-head-<pod-id>
```

### 6. Quick Health Check
```bash
# Wait for pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s

# Verify all containers running
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
```

### Expected Results
- **Head pod**: 2/2 Ready (ray-head + autoscaler containers)
- **Worker pods**: 1/1 Ready (ray-worker containers)  
- **No CrashLoopBackOff** if rayStartParams properly configured

### Troubleshooting
If pods still crash after redeploy:
1. Check autoscaler logs: `kubectl logs <head-pod> -c autoscaler`
2. Verify rayStartParams in YAML configuration
3. Check image pull issues: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`

### GPU processes linger after pod deletion

If `nvidia-smi` shows compute processes still running after pods are terminated/forced, the OS processes on the node have not been cleaned up.

Immediate remedies (node-level, requires root on the node):

```bash
# Map PID -> cgroup/container
sudo nvidia-smi pmon -s um
ps -p <PID> -o pid,ppid,cmd
sudo cat /proc/<PID>/cgroup

# Try graceful, then force kill
sudo kill -TERM <PID>
sleep 2
sudo kill -9 <PID>

# If no processes remain but GPU is still wedged, try GPU reset (supported on some GPUs/driver)
sudo nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i <GPU_ID>

# As a last resort, drain and reboot the node
kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
sudo reboot
```

Preventive measures (in cluster spec):
- Add a `preStop` lifecycle hook to Ray containers to run `ray stop` and TERM Python before exit.
- Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 120s) so Ray/UVicorn can release GPU contexts.
- Keep NVIDIA drivers/toolkit up to date; disable persistence mode if not required.

See the cluster YAML in this repo for an example of `lifecycle.preStop` on head and worker containers.

You’re right—force-deleting pods doesn’t guarantee GPU contexts get torn down. The container may vanish while the underlying process still holds a CUDA context, so nvidia-smi keeps showing it. Let’s fix it in two ways: immediate remediation on the node and a preventive, graceful shutdown in the cluster spec.

## Why this happens (quick)
- Force delete bypasses graceful shutdown. The Ray worker/python process can outlive the container teardown and keep the GPU context open.
- The NVIDIA device plugin can’t kill host processes; it only advertises/allocates devices.
- Result: orphaned compute processes linger until they’re terminated or the GPU/node is reset.

## Immediate remediation (node-level)
Requires root or sudo on the GPU node. Use this when you see lingering PIDs in nvidia-smi.

- Identify and map PIDs:
  - nvidia-smi pmon -s um
  - ps -p <PID> -o pid,ppid,cmd
  - cat /proc/<PID>/cgroup to find container/cgroup IDs
- Terminate:
  - kill -TERM <PID>, then kill -9 <PID> if needed
- If the GPU is still wedged (no processes but GPU won’t free):
  - nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i <GPU_ID> (if supported)
- Last resort:
  - kubectl cordon/drain the node, then reboot

I added these exact steps to

under “GPU processes linger after pod deletion” so it’s in your repo playbook.

## Preventive fix (graceful shutdown)
I updated your Ray cluster spec to give Ray a chance to release GPU contexts before termination:

- File:

- Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120 on head and worker pods
  - Added lifecycle.preStop to both containers:
    - Runs ray stop
    - Sends TERM to Python/Ray/ASGI processes
    - Small sleep to flush shutdown

This reduces the chance of orphaned GPU processes during rollouts or scale-downs.

What’s next
- Re-apply the RayService manifest so the lifecycle hooks take effect:
  - kubectl apply -f

- Wait for pods to roll and be Ready; if you hit hostPort scheduling again, use the forceful redeploy steps (the doc now covers GPU cleanup too).
- If you still see lingering PIDs after this change during future rollouts, we can:
  - Increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds a bit more
  - Add a preStop “best-effort” loop that waits until GPU usage drops (still unprivileged, but sometimes effective)
  - Consider removing hostPort to make rolling updates less brittle (not required for GPU cleanup but helps with scheduling smoothness)

Optional: If you want, I can also add a small “node debug/cleanup” snippet using kubectl debug --image and nsenter for environments without SSH, to help kill PIDs when required.

"""
Ray Serve deployment wrapper for EmbeddingService.

This module wraps the existing FastAPI application with Ray Serve
decorators to enable distributed deployment with autoscaling and
load balancing. No changes to the existing application logic required.
"""

from ray import serve

# Import the existing FastAPI app
from src.service.main import app


@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.2,  # Allow 2-5 replicas per GPU depending on model size
    },
    # Increase per-replica concurrency to tolerate larger bursts without Serve overload rejections.
    # Default is 5; previously 64; now 100 for additional headroom. Tune based on latency SLOs.
    max_ongoing_requests=100,
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    """
    Ray Serve deployment that wraps the FastAPI application.
    
    The @serve.ingress decorator makes all FastAPI routes available
    through Ray Serve, preserving all existing endpoints, middleware,
    and business logic without modification.
    """
    pass


# Deployment binding for Ray Serve
deployment = EmbeddingServiceDeployment.bind()

<attachment id="SERVICE_UPDATE_DEPLOY.md" filePath="/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/SERVICE_UPDATE_DEPLOY.md">
# Service Update & Deployment Guide

This guide walks you through rolling out a code/config change to the Embedding Service on Ray/Kubernetes, validating the rollout, and monitoring for regressions. It includes runnable command snippets and a couple of Mermaid sequence/flow diagrams for the big picture.

Links to related docs:
- `docs/headnode-log-discovery.md` — where to find Ray logs on head/worker nodes
- `docs/forceful-redeploy.md` — force a clean redeploy if needed
- `docs/ingress-nginx.md` — exposing the service externally via NGINX Ingress

---

## What changed (example)

In this rollout, we increased the per-replica concurrency to absorb ingress bursts without 500s from Serve overload rejections.

File: `src/service/ray_deployment.py`

```python
@serve.deployment(
    name="embedding-service",
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_cpus": 2,
        "num_gpus": 0.5,
    },
    # Raised from default (5) to 20 to reduce overload 500s during bursts
    max_ongoing_requests=20,
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,
        "max_replicas": 16,
        "target_num_ongoing_requests_per_replica": 4,
    },
)
@serve.ingress(app)
class EmbeddingServiceDeployment:
    pass
```

You can adapt these values to your traffic profile and resource budget.

---

## High-level rollout path

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Reg as Docker Registry
    participant K8s as K8s + KubeRay
    participant RS as RayService
    participant Pods as Ray Head/Workers
    participant Ing as NGINX Ingress
    participant Cl as Clients

    Dev->>Dev: Edit code/config
    Dev->>Reg: docker build && push new tag
    Dev->>K8s: kubectl apply -f RayService (new tag)
    K8s->>RS: Reconcile
    RS->>Pods: Create/Update head + workers + Serve app
    Cl-->>Ing: Send requests
    Ing-->>Pods: Forward to Serve proxy/replicas
    Pods-->>Cl: Responses
```

---

## Prerequisites

- kubectl context points to the right cluster/namespace (RayService lives in `default` by default)
- Access to your container registry (example below uses a local registry: `192.168.1.3:5000`)
- The RayService manifest at `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml`

---

## Step 1 — Build and push the image

Update the image tag as needed. Example uses `ray-latest-v2`.

```bash
docker build -t 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2 .
docker push 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2
```

If you version with a file (like `version`), bump it before the build.

---

## Step 2 — Point the RayService to the new image

Confirm your RayService uses the updated image (both head and workers). Example: `ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml` (snippet):

```yaml
spec:
  rayClusterConfig:
    headGroupSpec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: "192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2"
            imagePullPolicy: Always
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: worker-gpu
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:ray-latest-v2
            imagePullPolicy: Always
```

Apply the manifest:

```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl get rayservice -A -o wide
```

Note: A simple `apply` often triggers a rolling update. If ports/GPU reservations are stuck on the node, use a forceful redeploy (next section).

---

## Step 3 — Forceful redeploy (when in doubt)

If you see pods Pending due to hostPort collisions or GPU scheduling, follow `docs/forceful-redeploy.md`. Quick reference:

```bash
# Remove existing RayService (operator will clean up the cluster)
kubectl delete rayservice ray-cluster-simple --wait=true

# If any pods linger in Terminating, force delete them
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
kubectl delete pod <old-pod-names> --force --grace-period=0

# Recreate
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml

# Watch
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
```

Common Pending cause: “didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports” — resolve by ensuring old head/worker pods are fully removed (force delete if necessary).

---

## Step 4 — Wait for readiness

```bash
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -o wide
```

You should see the head pod Running with the expected ports and the worker pods Running (GPU ready if applicable).

---

## Step 5 — Quick health checks (via Ingress)

Set convenience variables to test through NGINX Ingress and nip.io (adapt to your env):

```bash
export NODE_IP=<your-node-ip>                 # e.g., 192.168.1.3
export NODE_PORT=<ingress-nodeport-http>      # e.g., 30333
export HOST=embeddings.${NODE_IP//./-}.nip.io
export ENDPOINT=http://$HOST:$NODE_PORT

curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health | jq .
curl -s -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"texts":["hello ingress"],"batch_size":32}' \
  $ENDPOINT/embeddings | jq .
```

---

## Step 6 — Burst test and summarize

Run a small burst (50 req, P=10) and summarize status codes and latency:

```bash
seq 50 | xargs -n1 -P 10 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code},%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Host: $HOST" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"texts":["hello world"]}' $ENDPOINT/embeddings | tee /tmp/burst.csv

awk -F, '{counts[$1]++} END{for (c in counts) printf("%s %d\n", c, counts[c])}' /tmp/burst.csv | sort
awk -F, '{sum+=$2; n++} END{printf("mean=%.4fs n=%d\n", sum/n, n)}' /tmp/burst.csv
cut -d, -f2 /tmp/burst.csv | sort -n | awk 'BEGIN{p50n=0;p95n=0} {vals[NR]=$1} END{n=NR;p50i=int(0.5*n); if(p50i<1)p50i=1; p95i=int(0.95*n); if(p95i<1)p95i=1; printf("p50=%.4fs p95=%.4fs count=%d\n", vals[p50i], vals[p95i], n)}'
```

Expected after the concurrency tweak: 200s across the board for this small burst; p50 ~20–40ms depending on model size and hardware.

---

## Step 7 — Monitor Ray logs (head + replicas)

See `docs/headnode-log-discovery.md` for more. Handy snippets:

```bash
HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# Serve proxy on the head
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log

# Per-replica logs on workers
for W in $(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=worker -o name); do
  kubectl exec ${W#pod/} -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_ || true
done

# Look for overload messages or exceptions
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- sh -lc "grep -RniE 'ERROR|Exception|Traceback|capacity' /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs | tail -n 200"
```

If you previously saw fast 500s during bursts, look for lines like:

```
WARNING replica.py:571 - Replica at capacity of max_ongoing_requests=5, rejecting request ...
```

After raising `max_ongoing_requests`, these should go away for the same burst level.

---

## Optional — Ingress retry & timeouts

You can smooth out brief backend hiccups by allowing limited retries at the ingress. Example annotations for your `Ingress` manifest:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "120"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream: "error timeout http_500 http_502 http_503 http_504"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-next-upstream-tries: "2"
```

Note: Retries on POST are generally “unsafe.” For idempotent embeddings this is typically acceptable—but validate with your product requirements.

---

## Rollback

If performance or error rates regress, roll back by pointing the RayService back to the previous image tag and re-apply. If pods hang on ports/GPUs, use the forceful redeploy steps.

```bash
# revert image tag in ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w
```

---

## Troubleshooting flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Apply new image/tag] --> B{Pods Pending?}
    B -- No --> C[Wait for Ready & test]
    B -- Yes --> D[Check Events: hostPort/GPU]
    D -->|hostPort in use| E[Force delete old pods]
    D -->|GPU not free| F[Drain/adjust resources]
    E --> G[Re-apply RayService]
    F --> G
    C --> H{Burst 500s?}
    H -- No --> I[Done]
    H -- Yes --> J[Check Serve logs for capacity]
    J -->|capacity rejects| K[Raise max_ongoing_requests or add replicas]
    J -->|exceptions| L[Fix app errors]
    K --> C
    L --> C
```

---

## Acceptance checklist

- RayService is Running; head/worker pods are Ready
- Health endpoint returns 200 via ingress
- Embeddings endpoint returns 200 for single request
- Burst test shows 0% 500s at your target concurrency (baseline P=10)
- No new warnings/errors in Serve proxy/replica logs

---

## Appendix — Frequently used commands

```bash
# Describe a problematic pod
kubectl describe pod <pod>

# Tail Serve controller/proxy logs on head
HEAD=$(kubectl get pods -l ray.io/node-type=head -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/controller_*.log
kubectl exec $HEAD -c ray-head -- tail -n 200 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve/proxy_*.log

# List per-replica logs on a worker
WORKER=<worker-pod>
kubectl exec $WORKER -c ray-worker -- ls -1 /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/serve | grep ^replica_

# Quick ingress health
curl -H "Host: $HOST" $ENDPOINT/health
```
</attachment>

# Headnode Log Discovery

## Quick Ray Cluster Health Check Process

### 1. Access Ray Session Logs
```bash
kubectl exec ray-cluster-simple-head-<pod-id> -c ray-head -- ls /tmp/ray/session_<timestamp>/logs/
```

### 2. Key Log Files & Purpose

| Log File | Purpose | Health Check |
|----------|---------|--------------|
| `gcs_server.out` | Cluster coordination, node registration | Check for registered nodes count |
| `raylet.out` | Worker process management | Look for remote node managers |
| `dashboard.log` | Web UI health | Verify 200 OK health responses |
| `dashboard_agent.log` | Local raylet health | Check raylet health endpoints |
| `monitor.log` | Autoscaler issues | **Critical**: Check for KeyError crashes |
| `runtime_env_agent.out` | Deployment dependencies | Verify running on port 60590 |
| `debug_state_gcs.txt` | Resource allocation summary | Check node/actor/placement counts |

### 3. Critical Commands
```bash
# Check cluster coordination
kubectl exec <head-pod> -c ray-head -- cat /tmp/ray/session_*/logs/gcs_server.out | tail -20

# Check autoscaler (most common failure)
kubectl exec <head-pod> -c ray-head -- tail -20 /tmp/ray/session_*/logs/monitor.log

# Verify worker connectivity
kubectl exec <head-pod> -c ray-head -- cat /tmp/ray/session_*/logs/raylet.out | tail -50

# Check resource state
kubectl exec <head-pod> -c ray-head -- head -50 /tmp/ray/session_*/logs/debug_state_gcs.txt
```

### 4. Common Issues & Fixes

**Autoscaler CrashLoopBackOff:**
- **Symptom**: `KeyError: 'rayStartParams'` in monitor.log
- **Fix**: Add `rayStartParams` to head and worker specs in ray-cluster YAML

**Cluster Health Indicators:**
- ✅ GCS shows 3+ registered nodes
- ✅ Dashboard returns 200 OK every few seconds  
- ✅ Raylet detects remote node managers
- ✅ Runtime env agent running on port 60590

### 5. Quick Status Check
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -5
```

**Healthy cluster**: Ray components running, only autoscaler may need rayStartParams fix.
