Set Up FastAPI and HTTP
This section helps you understand how to:

Send HTTP requests to Serve deployments
Use Ray Serve to integrate with FastAPI
Use customized HTTP adapters
Choose which feature to use for your use case
Set up keep alive timeout
Choosing the right HTTP feature

Serve offers a layered approach to expose your model with the right HTTP API.

Considering your use case, you can choose the right level of abstraction:

If you are comfortable working with the raw request object, use starlette.request.Requests API.
If you want a fully fledged API server with validation and doc generation, use the FastAPI integration.
Calling Deployments via HTTP

When you deploy a Serve application, the ingress deployment (the one passed to serve.run) is exposed over HTTP.

import starlette.requests
import requests
from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
class Counter:
    def __call__(self, request: starlette.requests.Request):
        return request.query_params


serve.run(Counter.bind())
resp = requests.get("http://localhost:8000?a=b&c=d")
assert resp.json() == {"a": "b", "c": "d"}

Requests to the Serve HTTP server at / are routed to the deployment’s __call__ method with a Starlette Request object as the sole argument. The __call__ method can return any JSON-serializable object or a Starlette Response object (e.g., to return a custom status code or custom headers). A Serve app’s route prefix can be changed from / to another string by setting route_prefix in serve.run() or the Serve config file.

Request cancellation

When processing a request takes longer than the end-to-end timeout or an HTTP client disconnects before receiving a response, Serve cancels the in-flight request:

If the proxy hasn’t yet sent the request to a replica, Serve simply drops the request.
If the request has been sent to a replica, Serve attempts to interrupt the replica and cancel the request. The asyncio.Task running the handler on the replica is cancelled, raising an asyncio.CancelledError the next time it enters an await statement. See the asyncio docs for more info. Handle this exception in a try-except block to customize your deployment’s behavior when a request is cancelled:
import asyncio
from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
async def startled():
    try:
        print("Replica received request!")
        await asyncio.sleep(10000)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        # Add custom behavior that should run
        # upon cancellation here.
        print("Request got cancelled!")

If no await statements are left in the deployment’s code before the request completes, the replica processes the request as usual, sends the response back to the proxy, and the proxy discards the response. Use await statements for blocking operations in a deployment, so Serve can cancel in-flight requests without waiting for the blocking operation to complete.

Cancellation cascades to any downstream deployment handle, task, or actor calls that were spawned in the deployment’s request-handling method. These can handle the asyncio.CancelledError in the same way as the ingress deployment.

To prevent an async call from being interrupted by asyncio.CancelledError, use asyncio.shield():

import asyncio
from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
class SnoringSleeper:
    async def snore(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print("ZZZ")

    async def __call__(self):
        try:
            print("SnoringSleeper received request!")

            # Prevent the snore() method from being cancelled
            await asyncio.shield(self.snore())

        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print("SnoringSleeper's request was cancelled!")


app = SnoringSleeper.bind()

When the request is cancelled, a cancellation error is raised inside the SnoringSleeper deployment’s __call__() method. However, the cancellation is not raised inside the snore() call, so ZZZ is printed even if the request is cancelled. Note that asyncio.shield cannot be used on a DeploymentHandle call to prevent the downstream handler from being cancelled. You need to explicitly handle the cancellation error in that handler as well.

FastAPI HTTP Deployments

If you want to define more complex HTTP handling logic, Serve integrates with FastAPI. This allows you to define a Serve deployment using the @serve.ingress decorator that wraps a FastAPI app with its full range of features. The most basic example of this is shown below, but for more details on all that FastAPI has to offer such as variable routes, automatic type validation, dependency injection (e.g., for database connections), and more, please check out their documentation.

Note
A Serve application that’s integrated with FastAPI still respects the route_prefix set through Serve. The routes that are registered through the FastAPI app object are layered on top of the route prefix. For instance, if your Serve application has route_prefix = /my_app and you decorate a method with @app.get("/fetch_data"), then you can call that method by sending a GET request to the path /my_app/fetch_data.
import ray
import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve

app = FastAPI()


@serve.deployment
@serve.ingress(app)
class MyFastAPIDeployment:
    @app.get("/")
    def root(self):
        return "Hello, world!"


serve.run(MyFastAPIDeployment.bind(), route_prefix="/hello")
resp = requests.get("http://localhost:8000/hello")
assert resp.json() == "Hello, world!"

Now if you send a request to /hello, this will be routed to the root method of our deployment. We can also easily leverage FastAPI to define multiple routes with different HTTP methods:

import ray
import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve

app = FastAPI()


@serve.deployment
@serve.ingress(app)
class MyFastAPIDeployment:
    @app.get("/")
    def root(self):
        return "Hello, world!"

    @app.post("/{subpath}")
    def root(self, subpath: str):
        return f"Hello from {subpath}!"


serve.run(MyFastAPIDeployment.bind(), route_prefix="/hello")
resp = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/hello/Serve")
assert resp.json() == "Hello from Serve!"

You can also pass in an existing FastAPI app to a deployment to serve it as-is:

import ray
import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def f():
    return "Hello from the root!"


@serve.deployment
@serve.ingress(app)
class FastAPIWrapper:
    pass


serve.run(FastAPIWrapper.bind(), route_prefix="/")
resp = requests.get("http://localhost:8000/")
assert resp.json() == "Hello from the root!"

This is useful for scaling out an existing FastAPI app with no modifications necessary. Existing middlewares, automatic OpenAPI documentation generation, and other advanced FastAPI features should work as-is.

WebSockets

Serve supports WebSockets via FastAPI:

from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

from ray import serve


app = FastAPI()


@serve.deployment
@serve.ingress(app)
class EchoServer:
    @app.websocket("/")
    async def echo(self, ws: WebSocket):
        await ws.accept()

        try:
            while True:
                text = await ws.receive_text()
                await ws.send_text(text)
        except WebSocketDisconnect:
            print("Client disconnected.")


serve_app = serve.run(EchoServer.bind())

Decorate the function that handles WebSocket requests with @app.websocket. Read more about FastAPI WebSockets in the FastAPI documentation.

Query the deployment using the websockets package (pip install websockets):

from websockets.sync.client import connect

with connect("ws://localhost:8000") as websocket:
    websocket.send("Eureka!")
    assert websocket.recv() == "Eureka!"

    websocket.send("I've found it!")
    assert websocket.recv() == "I've found it!"

FastAPI factory pattern

Ray Serve’s object-based pattern, shown previously, requires FastAPI objects to be serializable via cloudpickle, which prevents the use of some standard libraries like FastAPIInstrumentor due to their reliance on non-serializable components such as thread locks. The factory pattern create the object of FastAPI directly on each replica, avoiding the need for FastAPI object serialization.

import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.fastapi import FastAPIInstrumentor


@serve.deployment
class ChildDeployment:
    def __call__(self):
        return "Hello from the child deployment!"


def fastapi_factory():
    """Factory-style FastAPI app used as Serve ingress.

    We build the FastAPI app inside a factory and pass the callable to
    @serve.ingress.
    """
    app = FastAPI()

    # In an object-based ingress (where the FastAPI app is stored on the
    # deployment instance), Ray would need to serialize the app and its
    # instrumentation. Some instrumentors (like FastAPIInstrumentor) are not
    # picklable, which can cause serialization failures. Creating and
    # instrumenting the app here sidesteps that issue.
    FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app)

    @app.get("/")
    async def root():
        # Handlers defined inside this factory don't have access to the
        # ParentDeployment instance (i.e., there's no `self` here), so we
        # can't call `self.child`. Instead, fetch a handle by deployment name.
        handle = serve.get_deployment_handle("ChildDeployment", app_name="default")
        return {"message": await handle.remote()}

    return app


@serve.deployment
@serve.ingress(fastapi_factory)
class ParentDeployment:
    def __init__(self, child):
        self.child = child


serve.run(ParentDeployment.bind(ChildDeployment.bind()))

resp = requests.get("http://localhost:8000/")
assert resp.json() == {"message": "Hello from the child deployment!"}

Streaming Responses

Some applications must stream incremental results back to the caller. This is common for text generation using large language models (LLMs) or video processing applications. The full forward pass may take multiple seconds, so providing incremental results as they’re available provides a much better user experience.

To use HTTP response streaming, return a StreamingResponse that wraps a generator from your HTTP handler. This is supported for basic HTTP ingress deployments using a __call__ method and when using the FastAPI integration.

The code below defines a Serve application that incrementally streams numbers up to a provided max. The client-side code is also updated to handle the streaming outputs. This code uses the stream=True option to the requests library.

import time
from typing import Generator

import requests
from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse
from starlette.requests import Request

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
class StreamingResponder:
    def generate_numbers(self, max: int) -> Generator[str, None, None]:
        for i in range(max):
            yield str(i)
            time.sleep(0.1)

    def __call__(self, request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
        max = request.query_params.get("max", "25")
        gen = self.generate_numbers(int(max))
        return StreamingResponse(gen, status_code=200, media_type="text/plain")


serve.run(StreamingResponder.bind())

r = requests.get("http://localhost:8000?max=10", stream=True)
start = time.time()
r.raise_for_status()
for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=None, decode_unicode=True):
    print(f"Got result {round(time.time()-start, 1)}s after start: '{chunk}'")

Terminating the stream when a client disconnects

In some cases, you may want to cease processing a request when the client disconnects before the full stream has been returned. If you pass an async generator to StreamingResponse, it is cancelled and raises an asyncio.CancelledError when the client disconnects. Note that you must await at some point in the generator for the cancellation to occur.

In the example below, the generator streams responses forever until the client disconnects, then it prints that it was cancelled and exits. Save this code in stream.py and run it:

import asyncio
import time
from typing import AsyncGenerator

import requests
from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse
from starlette.requests import Request

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
class StreamingResponder:
    async def generate_forever(self) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
        try:
            i = 0
            while True:
                yield str(i)
                i += 1
                await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print("Cancelled! Exiting.")

    def __call__(self, request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
        gen = self.generate_forever()
        return StreamingResponse(gen, status_code=200, media_type="text/plain")


serve.run(StreamingResponder.bind())

r = requests.get("http://localhost:8000?max=10", stream=True)
start = time.time()
r.raise_for_status()
for i, chunk in enumerate(r.iter_content(chunk_size=None, decode_unicode=True)):
    print(f"Got result {round(time.time()-start, 1)}s after start: '{chunk}'")
    if i == 10:
        print("Client disconnecting")
        break

Set keep alive timeout

Serve uses a Uvicorn HTTP server internally to serve HTTP requests. By default, Uvicorn keeps HTTP connections alive for 5 seconds between requests. Modify the keep-alive timeout by setting the keep_alive_timeout_s in the http_options field of the Serve config files. This config is global to your Ray cluster, and you can’t update it during runtime. You can also set the RAY_SERVE_HTTP_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_S environment variable to set the keep alive timeout. RAY_SERVE_HTTP_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_S takes precedence over the keep_alive_timeout_s config if both are set. See Uvicorn’s keep alive timeout guide for more information.

  - Zero-downtime cluster upgrades (Step 8) with the stable head service selector automatically flipped
  - Stable serve service: `embedding-service-serve-svc` (Step 6: “rayservice-sample-serve-svc” in docs)
- Using the head service for dashboard and the serve service for traffic means your Ingress never needs to change across zero-downtime upgrades—the operator updates selectors to the new cluster.

- Optionally add `http_options: { location: EveryNode }` to `k8s/rayservice-local.yaml` if you want per-node proxies.
- Apply RayService + Ingress and verify Ready/Serve endpoints/Ingress 200s.

Ray Serve: Scalable and Programmable Serving
Production Guide
Custom Docker Images
Custom Docker Images
This section helps you:

Extend the official Ray Docker images with your own dependencies
Package your Serve application in a custom Docker image instead of a runtime_env
Use custom Docker images with KubeRay
To follow this tutorial, make sure to install Docker Desktop and create a Dockerhub account where you can host custom Docker images.

Working example#

Create a Python file called fake.py and save the following Serve application to it:

from faker import Faker

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
def create_fake_email():
    return Faker().email()


app = create_fake_email.bind()

This app creates and returns a fake email address. It relies on the Faker package to create the fake email address. Install the Faker package locally to run it:

pip install Faker==18.13.0

...

serve run fake:app

...

In another terminal window:
curl localhost:8000
john24@example.org

This tutorial explains how to package and serve this code inside a custom Docker image.

Extending the Ray Docker image

The rayproject organization maintains Docker images with dependencies needed to run Ray. In fact, the rayproject/ray repo hosts Docker images for this doc. For instance, this RayService config uses the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 image hosted by rayproject/ray.

You can extend these images and add your own dependencies to them by using them as a base layer in a Dockerfile. For instance, the working example application uses Ray 2.9.0 and Faker 18.13.0. You can create a Dockerfile that extends the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 by adding the Faker package:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

In general, the rayproject/ray images contain only the dependencies needed to import Ray and the Ray libraries. You can extend images from either of these repos to build your custom images.

Then, you can build this image and push it to your Dockerhub account, so it can be pulled in the future:

docker build . -t your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

docker image push your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

Make sure to replace your_dockerhub_username with your DockerHub user name and the custom_image_name with the name you want for your image. latest is this image’s version. If you don’t specify a version when you pull the image, then Docker automatically pulls the latest version of the package. You can also replace latest with a specific version if you prefer.

Adding your Serve application to the Docker image

During development, it’s useful to package your Serve application into a zip file and pull it into your Ray cluster using runtime_envs. During production, it’s more stable to put the Serve application in the Docker image instead of the runtime_env since new nodes won’t need to dynamically pull and install the Serve application code before running it.

Use the WORKDIR and COPY commands inside the Dockerfile to install the example Serve application code in your image:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

# Set the working dir for the container to /serve_app
WORKDIR /serve_app

# Copies the local `fake.py` file into the WORKDIR
COPY fake.py /serve_app/fake.py

KubeRay starts Ray with the ray start command inside the WORKDIR directory. All the Ray Serve actors are then able to import any dependencies in the directory. By COPYing the Serve file into the WORKDIR, the Serve deployments have access to the Serve code without needing a runtime_env.

For your applications, you can also add any other dependencies needed for your Serve app to the WORKDIR directory.

Build and push this image to Dockerhub. Use the same version as before to overwrite the image stored at that version.

Using custom Docker images in KubeRay

Run these custom Docker images in KubeRay by adding them to the RayService config. Make the following changes:

Set the rayVersion in the rayClusterConfig to the Ray version used in your custom Docker image.
Set the ray-head container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Set the ray-worker container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Update the serveConfigV2 field to remove any runtime_env dependencies that are in the container.
A pre-built version of this image is available at shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example. Try it out by running this RayService config:

apiVersion: ray.io/v1alpha1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: rayservice-fake-emails
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  serveConfigV2: |

Custom Docker Images
Custom Docker Images
This section helps you:

Extend the official Ray Docker images with your own dependencies
Package your Serve application in a custom Docker image instead of a runtime_env
Use custom Docker images with KubeRay
To follow this tutorial, make sure to install Docker Desktop and create a Dockerhub account where you can host custom Docker images.

Working example#

Create a Python file called fake.py and save the following Serve application to it:

from faker import Faker

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
def create_fake_email():
    return Faker().email()


app = create_fake_email.bind()

This app creates and returns a fake email address. It relies on the Faker package to create the fake email address. Install the Faker package locally to run it:

pip install Faker==18.13.0

...

serve run fake:app

...

In another terminal window:
curl localhost:8000
john24@example.org

This tutorial explains how to package and serve this code inside a custom Docker image.

Extending the Ray Docker image

The rayproject organization maintains Docker images with dependencies needed to run Ray. In fact, the rayproject/ray repo hosts Docker images for this doc. For instance, this RayService config uses the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 image hosted by rayproject/ray.

You can extend these images and add your own dependencies to them by using them as a base layer in a Dockerfile. For instance, the working example application uses Ray 2.9.0 and Faker 18.13.0. You can create a Dockerfile that extends the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 by adding the Faker package:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

In general, the rayproject/ray images contain only the dependencies needed to import Ray and the Ray libraries. You can extend images from either of these repos to build your custom images.

Then, you can build this image and push it to your Dockerhub account, so it can be pulled in the future:

docker build . -t your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

docker image push your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

Make sure to replace your_dockerhub_username with your DockerHub user name and the custom_image_name with the name you want for your image. latest is this image’s version. If you don’t specify a version when you pull the image, then Docker automatically pulls the latest version of the package. You can also replace latest with a specific version if you prefer.

Adding your Serve application to the Docker image

During development, it’s useful to package your Serve application into a zip file and pull it into your Ray cluster using runtime_envs. During production, it’s more stable to put the Serve application in the Docker image instead of the runtime_env since new nodes won’t need to dynamically pull and install the Serve application code before running it.

Use the WORKDIR and COPY commands inside the Dockerfile to install the example Serve application code in your image:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

# Set the working dir for the container to /serve_app
WORKDIR /serve_app

# Copies the local `fake.py` file into the WORKDIR
COPY fake.py /serve_app/fake.py

KubeRay starts Ray with the ray start command inside the WORKDIR directory. All the Ray Serve actors are then able to import any dependencies in the directory. By COPYing the Serve file into the WORKDIR, the Serve deployments have access to the Serve code without needing a runtime_env.

For your applications, you can also add any other dependencies needed for your Serve app to the WORKDIR directory.

Build and push this image to Dockerhub. Use the same version as before to overwrite the image stored at that version.

Using custom Docker images in KubeRay

Run these custom Docker images in KubeRay by adding them to the RayService config. Make the following changes:

Set the rayVersion in the rayClusterConfig to the Ray version used in your custom Docker image.
Set the ray-head container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Set the ray-worker container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Update the serveConfigV2 field to remove any runtime_env dependencies that are in the container.
A pre-built version of this image is available at shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example. Try it out by running this RayService config:

apiVersion: ray.io/v1alpha1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: rayservice-fake-emails
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: fake
        import_path: fake:app
        route_prefix: /
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.5.0' # Should match Ray version in the containers
    headGroupSpec:
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: ray-head
              image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
              resources:
                limits:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
                requests:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
              ports:
                - containerPort: 6379
                  name: gcs-server
                - containerPort: 8265 # Ray dashboard
                  name: dashboard
                - containerPort: 10001
                  name: client
                - containerPort: 8000
                  name: serve
    workerGroupSpecs:
      - replicas: 1
        minReplicas: 1
        maxReplicas: 1
        groupName: small-group
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
              - name: ray-worker
                image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
                lifecycle:
                  preStop:
                    exec:
                      command: ["/bin/sh","-c","ray stop"]
                resources:
                  limits:
                    cpu: "1"
                    memory: "2Gi"
                  requests:
                    cpu: "500m"

Custom Docker Images
Custom Docker Images
This section helps you:

Extend the official Ray Docker images with your own dependencies
Package your Serve application in a custom Docker image instead of a runtime_env
Use custom Docker images with KubeRay
To follow this tutorial, make sure to install Docker Desktop and create a Dockerhub account where you can host custom Docker images.

Working example#

Create a Python file called fake.py and save the following Serve application to it:

from faker import Faker

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
def create_fake_email():
    return Faker().email()


app = create_fake_email.bind()

This app creates and returns a fake email address. It relies on the Faker package to create the fake email address. Install the Faker package locally to run it:

pip install Faker==18.13.0

...

serve run fake:app

...

In another terminal window:
curl localhost:8000
john24@example.org

This tutorial explains how to package and serve this code inside a custom Docker image.

Extending the Ray Docker image

The rayproject organization maintains Docker images with dependencies needed to run Ray. In fact, the rayproject/ray repo hosts Docker images for this doc. For instance, this RayService config uses the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 image hosted by rayproject/ray.

You can extend these images and add your own dependencies to them by using them as a base layer in a Dockerfile. For instance, the working example application uses Ray 2.9.0 and Faker 18.13.0. You can create a Dockerfile that extends the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 by adding the Faker package:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

In general, the rayproject/ray images contain only the dependencies needed to import Ray and the Ray libraries. You can extend images from either of these repos to build your custom images.

Then, you can build this image and push it to your Dockerhub account, so it can be pulled in the future:

docker build . -t your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

docker image push your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

Make sure to replace your_dockerhub_username with your DockerHub user name and the custom_image_name with the name you want for your image. latest is this image’s version. If you don’t specify a version when you pull the image, then Docker automatically pulls the latest version of the package. You can also replace latest with a specific version if you prefer.

Adding your Serve application to the Docker image

During development, it’s useful to package your Serve application into a zip file and pull it into your Ray cluster using runtime_envs. During production, it’s more stable to put the Serve application in the Docker image instead of the runtime_env since new nodes won’t need to dynamically pull and install the Serve application code before running it.

Use the WORKDIR and COPY commands inside the Dockerfile to install the example Serve application code in your image:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

# Set the working dir for the container to /serve_app
WORKDIR /serve_app

# Copies the local `fake.py` file into the WORKDIR
COPY fake.py /serve_app/fake.py

KubeRay starts Ray with the ray start command inside the WORKDIR directory. All the Ray Serve actors are then able to import any dependencies in the directory. By COPYing the Serve file into the WORKDIR, the Serve deployments have access to the Serve code without needing a runtime_env.

For your applications, you can also add any other dependencies needed for your Serve app to the WORKDIR directory.

Build and push this image to Dockerhub. Use the same version as before to overwrite the image stored at that version.

Using custom Docker images in KubeRay

Run these custom Docker images in KubeRay by adding them to the RayService config. Make the following changes:

Set the rayVersion in the rayClusterConfig to the Ray version used in your custom Docker image.
Set the ray-head container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Set the ray-worker container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Update the serveConfigV2 field to remove any runtime_env dependencies that are in the container.
A pre-built version of this image is available at shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example. Try it out by running this RayService config:

apiVersion: ray.io/v1alpha1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: rayservice-fake-emails
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: fake
        import_path: fake:app
        route_prefix: /
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.5.0' # Should match Ray version in the containers
    headGroupSpec:
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: ray-head
              image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
              resources:
                limits:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
                requests:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
              ports:
                - containerPort: 6379
                  name: gcs-server
                - containerPort: 8265 # Ray dashboard
                  name: dashboard
                - containerPort: 10001
                  name: client
                - containerPort: 8000
                  name: serve
    workerGroupSpecs:
      - replicas: 1
        minReplicas: 1
        maxReplicas: 1
        groupName: small-group
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
              - name: ray-worker
                image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
                lifecycle:
                  preStop:
                    exec:
                      command: ["/bin/sh","-c","ray stop"]
                resources:
                  limits:
                    cpu: "1"
                    memory: "2Gi"
                  requests:
                    cpu: "500m"
                    memory: "2Gi"

# Ray Serve application configuration
  serveConfigV2: |
    http_options:
      host: "0.0.0.0"
      port: 8000
      location: EveryNode
    applications:
      - name: embedding-service
        import_path: src.service.ray_deployment:deployment
        route_prefix: "/"

# Head node - no GPU, used for coordination
    headGroupSpec:
      serviceType: ClusterIP
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
        num-cpus: '0'
      template:
        spec:
          terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
          containers:
          - name: ray-head
            image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:v4.0.1
            imagePullPolicy: Always  # Pull pinned image from local registry
            ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
              name: gcs
              protocol: TCP
            - containerPort: 8265
              name: dashboard
              protocol: TCP
            - containerPort: 10001
              name: client
              protocol: TCP
            - containerPort: 8000
              name: serve
              protocol: TCP
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "4"
                memory: "8Gi"
              requests:
                cpu: "2"
                memory: "4Gi"
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command:
                    - /bin/bash
                    - -lc
                    - |
                      echo "[preStop] Gracefully stopping Ray head...";
                      ray stop || true;
                      pkill -TERM -f "python.*ray" || true;
                      pkill -TERM -f "uvicorn|fastapi|gunicorn" || true;
                      sleep 5
            volumeMounts:
            - name: ray-storage
              mountPath: /mnt/ray-storage
            env:
            - name: RAY_STORAGE_PATH
              value: "/mnt/ray-storage"
            - name: TRANSFORMERS_CACHE
              value: "/root/.cache/huggingface"
          volumes:
          - name: ray-storage
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc

# Worker nodes - GPU enabled for embedding operations
    workerGroupSpecs:
    - groupName: worker-gpu
      replicas: 2
      minReplicas: 1
      maxReplicas: 4
      rayStartParams:
        num-gpus: '1'
      template:
        spec:
          terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
          containers:
          - name: ray-worker
            image: 192.168.1.3:5000/embedding-service:v4.0.1
            imagePullPolicy: Always  # Pull pinned image from local registry
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                  - bash
                  - -c
                  - wget --tries 1 -T 2 -q -O- http://localhost:52365/api/local_raylet_healthz | grep success
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
              periodSeconds: 5
              timeoutSeconds: 2
              failureThreshold: 3
            resources:
              limits:
                cpu: "6"
                memory: "12Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
              requests:
                cpu: "3"
                memory: "6Gi"
                nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
            lifecycle:
              preStop:
                exec:
                  command:
                    - /bin/bash
                    - -lc
                    - |
                      echo "[preStop] Gracefully stopping Ray worker...";
                      ray stop || true;
                      pkill -TERM -f "python.*ray" || true;
                      pkill -TERM -f "uvicorn|fastapi|gunicorn" || true;
                      sleep 5
            volumeMounts:
            - name: ray-storage
              mountPath: /mnt/ray-storage
            env:
            - name: RAY_STORAGE_PATH
              value: "/mnt/ray-storage"
            - name: TRANSFORMERS_CACHE
              value: "/root/.cache/huggingface"
            - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "all"
            - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
              value: "0"
          volumes:
          - name: ray-storage
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: ray-storage-pvc

Ray Serve: Scalable and Programmable Serving
Production Guide
Custom Docker Images
Custom Docker Images
This section helps you:

Extend the official Ray Docker images with your own dependencies
Package your Serve application in a custom Docker image instead of a runtime_env
Use custom Docker images with KubeRay
To follow this tutorial, make sure to install Docker Desktop and create a Dockerhub account where you can host custom Docker images.

Working example

Create a Python file called fake.py and save the following Serve application to it:

from faker import Faker

from ray import serve


@serve.deployment
def create_fake_email():
    return Faker().email()


app = create_fake_email.bind()

This app creates and returns a fake email address. It relies on the Faker package to create the fake email address. Install the Faker package locally to run it:

pip install Faker==18.13.0

...

serve run fake:app

...

In another terminal window:
curl localhost:8000
john24@example.org

This tutorial explains how to package and serve this code inside a custom Docker image.

Extending the Ray Docker image

The rayproject organization maintains Docker images with dependencies needed to run Ray. In fact, the rayproject/ray repo hosts Docker images for this doc. For instance, this RayService config uses the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 image hosted by rayproject/ray.

You can extend these images and add your own dependencies to them by using them as a base layer in a Dockerfile. For instance, the working example application uses Ray 2.9.0 and Faker 18.13.0. You can create a Dockerfile that extends the rayproject/ray:2.9.0 by adding the Faker package:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

In general, the rayproject/ray images contain only the dependencies needed to import Ray and the Ray libraries. You can extend images from either of these repos to build your custom images.

Then, you can build this image and push it to your Dockerhub account, so it can be pulled in the future:

docker build . -t your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

docker image push your_dockerhub_username/custom_image_name:latest

...

Make sure to replace your_dockerhub_username with your DockerHub user name and the custom_image_name with the name you want for your image. latest is this image’s version. If you don’t specify a version when you pull the image, then Docker automatically pulls the latest version of the package. You can also replace latest with a specific version if you prefer.

Adding your Serve application to the Docker image

During development, it’s useful to package your Serve application into a zip file and pull it into your Ray cluster using runtime_envs. During production, it’s more stable to put the Serve application in the Docker image instead of the runtime_env since new nodes won’t need to dynamically pull and install the Serve application code before running it.

Use the WORKDIR and COPY commands inside the Dockerfile to install the example Serve application code in your image:

# File name: Dockerfile
FROM rayproject/ray:2.9.0

RUN pip install Faker==18.13.0

# Set the working dir for the container to /serve_app
WORKDIR /serve_app

# Copies the local `fake.py` file into the WORKDIR
COPY fake.py /serve_app/fake.py

KubeRay starts Ray with the ray start command inside the WORKDIR directory. All the Ray Serve actors are then able to import any dependencies in the directory. By COPYing the Serve file into the WORKDIR, the Serve deployments have access to the Serve code without needing a runtime_env.

For your applications, you can also add any other dependencies needed for your Serve app to the WORKDIR directory.

Build and push this image to Dockerhub. Use the same version as before to overwrite the image stored at that version.

Using custom Docker images in KubeRay

Run these custom Docker images in KubeRay by adding them to the RayService config. Make the following changes:

Set the rayVersion in the rayClusterConfig to the Ray version used in your custom Docker image.
Set the ray-head container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Set the ray-worker container’s image to the custom image’s name on Dockerhub.
Update the serveConfigV2 field to remove any runtime_env dependencies that are in the container.
A pre-built version of this image is available at shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example. Try it out by running this RayService config:

apiVersion: ray.io/v1alpha1
kind: RayService
metadata:
  name: rayservice-fake-emails
spec:
  serviceUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  deploymentUnhealthySecondThreshold: 300
  serveConfigV2: |
    applications:
      - name: fake
        import_path: fake:app
        route_prefix: /
  rayClusterConfig:
    rayVersion: '2.5.0' # Should match Ray version in the containers
    headGroupSpec:
      rayStartParams:
        dashboard-host: '0.0.0.0'
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: ray-head
              image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
              resources:
                limits:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
                requests:
                  cpu: 2
                  memory: 2Gi
              ports:
                - containerPort: 6379
                  name: gcs-server
                - containerPort: 8265 # Ray dashboard
                  name: dashboard
                - containerPort: 10001
                  name: client
                - containerPort: 8000
                  name: serve
    workerGroupSpecs:
      - replicas: 1
        minReplicas: 1
        maxReplicas: 1
        groupName: small-group
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
              - name: ray-worker
                image: shrekrisanyscale/serve-fake-email-example:example
                lifecycle:
                  preStop:
                    exec:
                      command: ["/bin/sh","-c","ray stop"]
                resources:
                  limits:
                    cpu: "1"
                    memory: "2Gi"
                  requests:
                    cpu: "500m"
                    memory: "2Gi"

<attachment id="forceful-redeploy.md" filePath="/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/docs/forceful-redeploy.md">
# Forceful Redeploy

## Quick Ray Cluster Forced Redeployment Process

### 1. Delete Current Deployment
```bash
kubectl delete raycluster ray-cluster-simple
```

### 2. Force Delete Stuck Pods (if needed)
```bash
# Check for terminating pods
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple

# Force delete if stuck in Terminating state
kubectl delete pod ray-cluster-simple-head-* ray-cluster-simple-worker-* --force --grace-period=0
```

### 3. Verify Clean State
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
# Should return "No resources found"
```

### 4. Redeploy with Updated Configuration
```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
```

### 5. Monitor New Deployment
```bash
# Watch pod creation
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w

# Check specific pod status
kubectl describe pod ray-cluster-simple-head-<pod-id>
```

### 6. Quick Health Check
```bash
# Wait for pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s

# Verify all containers running
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
```

### Expected Results
- **Head pod**: 2/2 Ready (ray-head + autoscaler containers)
- **Worker pods**: 1/1 Ready (ray-worker containers)  
- **No CrashLoopBackOff** if rayStartParams properly configured

### Troubleshooting
If pods still crash after redeploy:
1. Check autoscaler logs: `kubectl logs <head-pod> -c autoscaler`
2. Verify rayStartParams in YAML configuration
3. Check image pull issues: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`

### GPU processes linger after pod deletion

If `nvidia-smi` shows compute processes still running after pods are terminated/forced, the OS processes on the node have not been cleaned up.

Immediate remedies (node-level, requires root on the node):

```bash
# Map PID -> cgroup/container
sudo nvidia-smi pmon -s um
ps -p <PID> -o pid,ppid,cmd
sudo cat /proc/<PID>/cgroup

# Try graceful, then force kill
sudo kill -TERM <PID>
sleep 2
sudo kill -9 <PID>

# If no processes remain but GPU is still wedged, try GPU reset (supported on some GPUs/driver)
sudo nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i <GPU_ID>

# As a last resort, drain and reboot the node
kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
sudo reboot
```

Preventive measures (in cluster spec):
- Add a `preStop` lifecycle hook to Ray containers to run `ray stop` and TERM Python before exit.
- Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 120s) so Ray/UVicorn can release GPU contexts.
- Keep NVIDIA drivers/toolkit up to date; disable persistence mode if not required.

See the cluster YAML in this repo for an example of `lifecycle.preStop` on head and worker containers.

<attachment id="forceful-redeploy.md" filePath="/home/electric/workspace/EmbeddingService/docs/forceful-redeploy.md">
# Forceful Redeploy

## Quick Ray Cluster Forced Redeployment Process

### 1. Delete Current Deployment
```bash
kubectl delete raycluster ray-cluster-simple
```

### 2. Force Delete Stuck Pods (if needed)
```bash
# Check for terminating pods
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple

# Force delete if stuck in Terminating state
kubectl delete pod ray-cluster-simple-head-* ray-cluster-simple-worker-* --force --grace-period=0
```

### 3. Verify Clean State
```bash
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
# Should return "No resources found"
```

### 4. Redeploy with Updated Configuration
```bash
kubectl apply -f ray-cluster-dual-workers.yaml
```

### 5. Monitor New Deployment
```bash
# Watch pod creation
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple -w

# Check specific pod status
kubectl describe pod ray-cluster-simple-head-<pod-id>
```

### 6. Quick Health Check
```bash
# Wait for pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple --timeout=300s

# Verify all containers running
kubectl get pods -l ray.io/cluster=ray-cluster-simple
```

### Expected Results
- **Head pod**: 2/2 Ready (ray-head + autoscaler containers)
- **Worker pods**: 1/1 Ready (ray-worker containers)  
- **No CrashLoopBackOff** if rayStartParams properly configured

### Troubleshooting
If pods still crash after redeploy:
1. Check autoscaler logs: `kubectl logs <head-pod> -c autoscaler`
2. Verify rayStartParams in YAML configuration
3. Check image pull issues: `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`

### GPU processes linger after pod deletion

If `nvidia-smi` shows compute processes still running after pods are terminated/forced, the OS processes on the node have not been cleaned up.

Immediate remedies (node-level, requires root on the node):

```bash
# Map PID -> cgroup/container
sudo nvidia-smi pmon -s um
ps -p <PID> -o pid,ppid,cmd
sudo cat /proc/<PID>/cgroup

# Try graceful, then force kill
sudo kill -TERM <PID>
sleep 2
sudo kill -9 <PID>

# If no processes remain but GPU is still wedged, try GPU reset (supported on some GPUs/driver)
sudo nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i <GPU_ID>

# As a last resort, drain and reboot the node
kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
sudo reboot
```

Preventive measures (in cluster spec):
- Add a `preStop` lifecycle hook to Ray containers to run `ray stop` and TERM Python before exit.
- Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (e.g., 120s) so Ray/UVicorn can release GPU contexts.
- Keep NVIDIA drivers/toolkit up to date; disable persistence mode if not required.

See the cluster YAML in this repo for an example of `lifecycle.preStop` on head and worker containers.

- **100 requests @ concurrency 10**: 100% success (100/100), mean 0.0836s

Let's check the current rate limiting configuration in our Ray deployment:
Now let's also check the FastAPI application level rate limiting:
Let me check the semaphore limits configuration:

per replica (so 200 total across 2 workers)
- Application level: `embedding_requests: 8` per replica (so 16 total across 2 workers)

The `embedding_requests` semaphore of 8 per replica is the real bottleneck. For segmentation workloads with 2 workers, we should increase this limit. Let's compare this with the non-segmentation test we ran earlier:

# Load Testing Optimization Guide

The EmbeddingService is a production-ready Ray Serve deployment that provides scalable text embedding capabilities with advanced features like semantic segmentation. This guide covers comprehensive load testing strategies, performance optimization techniques, and deployment best practices for multi-worker Ray clusters.

The service architecture leverages Ray's distributed computing framework to provide horizontal scaling across multiple GPU workers, while implementing sophisticated rate limiting and resource management to ensure stability under high load conditions. The core embedding functionality is built around transformer models with custom tokenization handling and memory-efficient batch processing.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Basic load test (non-segmentation)
python3 working_dir/load_test.py --url http://embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io:30333 --requests 1000 --concurrency 20 --segmentation false

# Segmentation load test (compute-intensive)
python3 working_dir/load_test.py --url http://embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io:30333 --requests 500 --concurrency 10 --segmentation true

# High-volume stress test
python3 working_dir/load_test.py --url http://embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io:30333 --requests 10000 --concurrency 10 --segmentation true
```

The load testing script (`working_dir/load_test.py`) is designed to simulate realistic production workloads with configurable parameters for request volume, concurrency patterns, and payload complexity. It uses Python's `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` to generate concurrent HTTP requests while collecting detailed performance metrics including status code distributions, latency percentiles, and throughput measurements.

## Architecture Overview

The EmbeddingService implements a sophisticated multi-tier architecture that combines Ray Serve's distributed computing capabilities with FastAPI's high-performance web framework. The system is designed to handle both lightweight embedding requests and compute-intensive segmentation workloads across multiple GPU-enabled worker nodes.

The deployment architecture centers around the Ray cluster configuration defined in `k8s/rayservice-local.yaml`, which orchestrates a head node for coordination and multiple worker nodes for parallel processing. Each worker node is equipped with NVIDIA RTX A4500 GPUs and runs the embedding engine defined in `src/components/embedding_engine.py`. The Ray Serve framework automatically handles load balancing, request routing, and fault tolerance across these distributed components.

The ingress layer uses NGINX (`helm/nginx-ingress/embedding-service-ingress.yaml`) to provide external HTTP/HTTPS access with intelligent routing based on host headers. This configuration supports both development testing via NodePort and production deployment with LoadBalancer service types, ensuring seamless traffic distribution to the underlying Ray Serve HTTP proxies.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Client Requests] --> B[NGINX Ingress]
    B --> C[embedding-service-serve-svc]
    C --> D[Ray Serve HTTP Proxy]
    D --> E[Ray Serve Deployment]
    E --> F[FastAPI Application]
    F --> G[Semaphore Limits]
    G --> H[Embedding Engine]
    
    subgraph "Rate Limiting Layers"
        I[1. NGINX Rate Limiting]
        J[2. Ray Serve max_ongoing_requests]
        K[3. Application Semaphores]
        L[4. GPU Memory Constraints]
    end
    
    D -.-> I
    E -.-> J
    F -.-> K
    H -.-> L
```

The service implements four distinct layers of rate limiting and resource management. At the infrastructure level, NGINX provides basic request throttling and connection limiting. Ray Serve enforces deployment-level concurrency controls through the `max_ongoing_requests` parameter, which is configured in `src/service/ray_deployment.py`. The application layer implements fine-grained semaphore-based throttling defined in `src/config.py`, allowing precise control over different endpoint types. Finally, GPU memory constraints provide a natural upper bound on concurrent processing capacity.

## Request Flow Sequence

Understanding the complete request lifecycle is crucial for optimizing performance and diagnosing bottlenecks. The service processes requests through a carefully orchestrated sequence that involves multiple components, each with specific responsibilities and potential failure points.

When a client initiates a request, it first encounters the NGINX Ingress controller configured in `helm/nginx-ingress/embedding-service-ingress.yaml`. This component handles SSL termination, host-based routing, and initial request validation. The ingress configuration includes optimized proxy timeouts (`proxy_read_timeout`, `proxy_send_timeout`) and buffering settings (`proxy_buffering`, `client_max_body_size`) tuned for embedding workloads that may involve large text payloads.

The request then flows to the Ray Serve HTTP proxy, which implements the `location: EveryNode` configuration. This setting ensures that HTTP proxies are distributed across all worker nodes rather than centralized on the head node, providing better load distribution and eliminating single points of failure. The Ray Serve layer also implements autoscaling logic defined in `src/service/ray_deployment.py`, dynamically adjusting the number of active replicas based on request volume and response times.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant N as NGINX Ingress
    participant RS as Ray Serve
    participant FA as FastAPI App
    participant S as Semaphore
    participant EE as Embedding Engine
    participant GPU as GPU
    
    C->>N: HTTP Request
    N->>RS: Forward to Ray Serve
    RS->>FA: Route to FastAPI
    FA->>S: Acquire semaphore
    alt Semaphore Available
        S-->>FA: Acquired
        FA->>EE: Process embeddings
        EE->>GPU: Model inference
        GPU-->>EE: Embeddings result
        EE-->>FA: Return embeddings
        FA->>S: Release semaphore
        S-->>FA: Released
        FA-->>RS: HTTP 200 + embeddings
        RS-->>N: Response
        N-->>C: HTTP 200
    else Semaphore Exhausted
        S-->>FA: Rejected
        FA-->>RS: HTTP 429 Rate Limited
        RS-->>N: HTTP 429
        N-->>C: HTTP 429
    end
```

At the application level, the FastAPI framework defined in `src/service/main.py` coordinates request processing through a series of middleware components. The error handling middleware (`src/service/middleware/error_handler.py`) provides structured exception management and logging, while the validation middleware (`src/service/middleware/validation.py`) ensures request schemas conform to expected formats defined in `src/service/schemas/requests.py`.

The core processing logic resides in the embedding engine (`src/components/embedding_engine.py`), which implements thread-safe tokenization using locks to prevent concurrent access issues with Hugging Face transformers. This component handles model loading, batch processing optimization, and GPU memory management. The engine supports both standard embedding generation and advanced segmentation processing, where text is intelligently split into semantic chunks before embedding generation.

## Rate Limiting Configuration Layers

The EmbeddingService implements a sophisticated multi-layer rate limiting strategy that provides granular control over resource utilization while maintaining system stability under varying load conditions. Each layer serves a specific purpose in the overall performance management strategy, from coarse-grained infrastructure controls to fine-grained application-level resource management.

### 1. Ray Serve Level (`src/service/ray_deployment.py`)

The Ray Serve configuration represents the primary orchestration layer for distributed request handling. The deployment decorator in `src/service/ray_deployment.py` defines critical parameters that control how requests are distributed across worker replicas and how the system responds to varying load conditions.

```python
@serve.deployment(
    # Primary rate limiting - controls concurrent requests per replica
    max_ongoing_requests=100,  # ← Key parameter for Ray-level throttling
    
    # Auto-scaling configuration
    autoscaling_config={
        "min_replicas": 2,     # Minimum worker replicas
        "max_replicas": 4,     # Maximum worker replicas
        "target_ongoing_requests": 50,  # Target load per replica
    },
    
    # Resource allocation
    ray_actor_options={
        "num_gpus": 1,         # GPU allocation per replica
        "num_cpus": 4,         # CPU allocation per replica
    }
)
```

The `max_ongoing_requests` parameter is particularly critical as it defines the upper bound for concurrent request processing at each replica. This setting directly impacts memory consumption patterns and GPU utilization efficiency. When this limit is reached, Ray Serve will queue additional requests rather than overwhelming individual workers, providing natural backpressure that prevents out-of-memory conditions.

The autoscaling configuration works in conjunction with the resource allocation settings to provide dynamic capacity management. The `target_ongoing_requests` parameter triggers scaling decisions - when the average request load per replica exceeds this threshold, Ray Serve will attempt to spawn additional replicas up to the `max_replicas` limit. This mechanism ensures that the system can adapt to traffic spikes while maintaining predictable resource usage patterns.

**Optimization Impact:**
- `max_ongoing_requests`: Higher values = more concurrent processing but higher memory usage
- `target_ongoing_requests`: Lower values = more aggressive scaling but more resource overhead

### 2. Application Semaphore Limits (`src/config.py`)

The application-level semaphore system provides the most granular control over concurrent request processing. Unlike Ray Serve's deployment-level controls, these semaphores operate at the individual endpoint level, allowing for differentiated resource allocation based on the computational complexity of different operations.

```python
# Current configuration
SEMAPHORE_LIMITS = {
    "embedding_requests": 8,        # ← Primary bottleneck for segmentation
    "similarity_requests": 10,
    "model_requests": 5,
    "batch_requests": 3,            # For batch processing
}

# Proposed optimization for 2-worker setup
SEMAPHORE_LIMITS = {
    "embedding_requests": 16,       # Doubled for 2-worker deployment
    "similarity_requests": 20,      # Increased proportionally
    "model_requests": 10,           # Doubled
    "batch_requests": 6,            # Doubled
}
```

The semaphore implementation in `src/service/core/dependencies.py` uses asyncio-based resource management to ensure that the number of concurrent operations never exceeds safe thresholds. Each endpoint type has its own semaphore pool, allowing for fine-tuned control over resource allocation. For example, embedding requests (which involve heavy GPU computation) have more restrictive limits compared to similarity requests (which primarily involve vector operations).

The segmentation functionality, accessible through the `/embeddings` endpoint with `use_segmentation=true`, represents the most computationally intensive operation. This feature, implemented in the embedding engine, performs intelligent text splitting before generating embeddings for each segment. The computational overhead is significantly higher than standard embedding generation, requiring careful semaphore tuning to prevent system overload.

**Calculation Logic:**
```python
# Base limits designed for single worker
base_embedding_requests = 8

# Scale with number of workers
num_workers = 2
optimized_limit = base_embedding_requests * num_workers

# Apply safety factor for GPU memory
safety_factor = 1.0  # Conservative for RTX A4500
final_limit = int(optimized_limit * safety_factor)
```

The calculation logic considers both the number of available workers and the GPU memory characteristics of the deployment hardware. RTX A4500 GPUs provide substantial memory capacity (16GB), but transformer models can consume variable amounts of memory depending on input text length and batch size. The safety factor allows for conservative resource allocation that prevents out-of-memory conditions even under peak load scenarios.

### 3. HTTP Configuration (`k8s/rayservice-local.yaml`)

The Kubernetes deployment manifest defines the foundational infrastructure configuration that supports the distributed Ray cluster. The RayService custom resource in `k8s/rayservice-local.yaml` orchestrates both the Ray cluster topology and the Serve application configuration, providing a declarative approach to managing complex distributed deployments.

```yaml
serveConfigV2: |
  http_options:
    location: EveryNode          # Distribute HTTP proxies across all nodes
    port: 8000
  applications:
  - name: embedding-service
    route_prefix: "/"
    import_path: src.service.main:deployment
```

The `location: EveryNode` configuration represents a critical architectural decision that significantly impacts load balancing performance. By default, Ray Serve centralizes HTTP proxies on the head node, creating a potential bottleneck for high-throughput scenarios. The EveryNode setting distributes HTTP proxy instances across all worker nodes, enabling direct request routing to the node that will ultimately process the request.

This configuration works synergistically with the NGINX Ingress controller to provide optimal request distribution. The service discovery mechanism automatically updates the `embedding-service-serve-svc` Kubernetes service with endpoints representing all active HTTP proxies. The load balancing algorithms can then distribute incoming requests directly to worker nodes without introducing additional network hops through the head node.

The manifest also includes sophisticated lifecycle management configuration, including `preStop` hooks that ensure graceful shutdown during scaling operations. This is particularly important for GPU workloads where abrupt termination can leave CUDA contexts in inconsistent states. The readiness probes are configured to check the Ray dashboard's healthz endpoint, ensuring that workers are not marked as ready until the Ray runtime is fully initialized.

**Benefits of `location: EveryNode`:**
- Load balancing across all worker nodes
- Reduced head node bottleneck
- Better fault tolerance
- Improved network efficiency for large deployments

The manifest supports both static worker configurations for predictable workloads and autoscaling configurations for variable demand patterns. The worker group specifications include resource requests and limits that ensure proper Kubernetes scheduling while providing guaranteed access to GPU resources. The resource management also includes CPU and memory allocations tuned for transformer model inference workloads.

### 4. Container and Infrastructure Configuration

The containerization strategy defined in `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.base` implements a multi-stage build process optimized for both development velocity and production efficiency. The base image includes CUDA runtime components, PyTorch, and Ray dependencies, while the application image adds the embedding service code and specific model artifacts.

The build process leverages Docker layer caching to minimize rebuild times during development cycles. The `Makefile` provides standardized build and deployment commands that ensure consistent image tagging and registry management across different environments. The version management system (`version` file) enables automated image tagging that supports both semantic versioning and git commit-based identification.

Container resource management is coordinated between the Docker runtime, Kubernetes resource specifications, and Ray's internal resource allocation. The configuration ensures that GPU devices are properly exposed to containers while maintaining isolation between different Ray actors running on the same node.

## Load Testing Script Analysis

The load testing framework implemented in `working_dir/load_test.py` provides comprehensive performance validation capabilities designed specifically for embedding service workloads. The script implements a thread-based concurrent testing approach that closely simulates real-world client behavior while collecting detailed performance metrics for analysis and optimization.

### Script Architecture and Design

The load testing script employs Python's `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` to generate realistic concurrent load patterns. Unlike simple sequential testing, this approach creates genuine contention for resources and accurately reflects the behavior of multiple clients accessing the service simultaneously. The script carefully manages connection pooling and request lifecycle to ensure that performance measurements reflect actual service behavior rather than client-side limitations.

The script supports two primary operational modes corresponding to the service's main use cases. Standard embedding requests (`segmentation=false`) represent the most common workload, involving straightforward text-to-vector transformation using pre-trained transformer models. Segmentation requests (`segmentation=true`) represent compute-intensive workloads that perform intelligent text splitting before generating embeddings for each segment, resulting in significantly higher computational requirements and different performance characteristics.

### Script Parameters

```python
# Core parameters
--url: str              # Base URL (without /embeddings suffix)
--requests: int         # Total number of requests to send
--concurrency: int      # Number of concurrent threads
--segmentation: bool    # Enable compute-intensive segmentation

# Example usage patterns
basic_test = {
    "requests": 100,
    "concurrency": 10,
    "segmentation": False,
    "expected": "100% success rate"
}

stress_test = {
    "requests": 1000,
    "concurrency": 20,
    "segmentation": False,
    "expected": "95-99% success rate"
}

segmentation_test = {
    "requests": 500,
    "concurrency": 10,
    "segmentation": True,
    "expected": "50-80% success rate (compute limited)"
}
```

The parameter selection reflects different testing scenarios that correspond to real-world usage patterns. Basic tests validate fundamental functionality and provide baseline performance measurements. Stress tests identify breaking points and resource limitations under sustained high load. Segmentation tests specifically validate the service's ability to handle compute-intensive workloads that may require different resource allocation strategies.

The script's request generation logic creates realistic payloads that reflect actual embedding service usage. The default test payload includes a moderately long text sample (repeated 20 times to create substantial content), along with shorter text variations to simulate mixed batch processing scenarios. This approach ensures that performance measurements account for the variable computational requirements of different text lengths and complexities.

### Metrics Collection and Analysis

The script implements comprehensive metrics collection that goes beyond simple success/failure tracking. Response time measurements capture the complete request lifecycle, including network latency, queue waiting time, and actual processing time. The percentile calculations (p50, p95, p99) provide insight into latency distribution patterns that are critical for understanding user experience under different load conditions.

```python
# Example implementation of metrics collection
def post_json(url: str, payload: dict, timeout: float = 30.0):
    data = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=data, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST")
    start = time.time()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
            status = resp.getcode()
            _ = resp.read()  # drain response body
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        status = e.code
    except Exception:
        status = 0  # Network or other error
    latency = time.time() - start
    return status, latency
```

The status code distribution analysis provides insight into different types of service responses. A predominance of 200 responses indicates healthy operation, while 429 responses indicate rate limiting activation. Other status codes (500, 503) may indicate resource exhaustion or configuration problems that require investigation.

### Script Output Analysis

```python
# Output format

status-dist: 429:8800, 200:1200
mean: 0.0297s p50: 0.0200s p95: 0.0791s p99: 0.4643s

# Interpretation
success_rate = 200_count / total_requests  # 12% in this example
rate_limited = 429_count / total_requests  # 88% rate limited
p95_latency = 0.0791  # 95th percentile response time
```

The output interpretation requires understanding the relationship between different metrics and their implications for service performance. Success rates below 95% for non-segmentation workloads typically indicate resource constraints or configuration issues. However, for segmentation workloads, lower success rates may be expected due to the higher computational requirements.

Latency distribution analysis helps identify performance patterns and potential optimization opportunities. Consistent low latencies (p50 ≈ p95) indicate predictable performance, while large gaps between percentiles suggest variable processing times that may indicate resource contention or inefficient batching strategies.

### Integration with Deployment Infrastructure

The load testing script integrates seamlessly with the service's deployment infrastructure through the NGINX Ingress configuration. The script can target either direct service endpoints (for internal testing) or external ingress endpoints (for end-to-end validation). The host header configuration (`Host: embeddings.192-168-1-3.nip.io`) enables testing through the complete request routing pipeline, including NGINX proxy handling and load balancing across worker nodes.

The script also supports different deployment topologies, from single-worker development environments to multi-worker production clusters. The same testing methodology can validate performance characteristics across different scaling configurations, helping identify optimal worker counts and resource allocation strategies for specific workload patterns.

## Performance Benchmarks The performance benchmarking results provide critical insights into the service's behavior under different load conditions and configuration parameters. These measurements were collected using the standardized load testing methodology with a 2-worker Ray cluster deployment, each worker equipped with NVIDIA RTX A4500 GPUs and configured with the current conservative semaphore limits. ### Current Results (2 Workers, Conservative Limits) The benchmark data reveals distinct performance characteristics for different workload types, highlighting the impact of computational complexity on throughput and resource utilization patterns. | Test Type | Requests | Concurrency | Success Rate | P95 Latency | Analysis | |-----------|----------|-------------|--------------|-------------|----------| | Basic | 100 | 10 | 100% | 0.26s | Optimal | | Standard | 1000 | 20 | 99% | 0.28s | Excellent | | Segmentation | 500 | 15 | 2% | 0.08s | Bottleneck | | High-Volume Seg | 10000 | 10 | 12% | 0.08s | Severe bottleneck | The basic and standard test results demonstrate excellent performance characteristics for non-segmentation workloads. The 99-100% success rates indicate that the current configuration can handle substantial concurrent load for standard embedding generation tasks. The consistent latency patterns (p95 around 0.26-0.28s) suggest predictable performance that would provide good user experience in production scenarios. However, the segmentation test results reveal a significant performance constraint. With only 2-12% success rates for segmentation workloads, the majority of requests are being rate-limited rather than processed. This pattern indicates that the current semaphore configuration is too conservative for the available computational resources in a 2-worker deployment. ### Workload Characteristics Analysis The performance differential between standard and segmentation workloads reflects the underlying computational complexity differences. Standard embedding generation involves a single forward pass through the transformer model, with computational complexity primarily determined by input text length and batch size. The consistent high success rates indicate that the current resource allocation is well-suited for this workload type. Segmentation workloads involve multiple processing stages: intelligent text splitting using natural language processing techniques, individual embedding generation for each segment, and result aggregation. This multi-stage processing requires significantly more CPU and GPU resources per request, explaining the dramatic performance differences observed in the benchmarks. The latency measurements for segmentation requests show interesting patterns. Despite the low success rates, the actual processing times for successful requests remain quite low (p95 ≈ 0.08s). This suggests that the bottleneck is not in the computational processing itself, but rather in the resource allocation and queuing mechanisms that prevent requests from reaching the processing stage. ### Bottleneck Analysis ```mermaid graph LR A[Request] --> B{Ray Serve

The current configuration allows only 8 concurrent embedding requests per replica, resulting in a maximum of 16 concurrent segmentation requests across the entire 2-worker cluster. This limit is significantly below the computational capacity of the available GPU resources. **Current Bottleneck:** Application semaphore `embedding_requests: 8` per replica - 2 workers × 8 requests = 16 concurrent segmentation requests maximum - With 10000 requests at concurrency 10, queue buildup causes 88% rate limiting The Ray Serve layer (`max_ongoing_requests: 100` per replica) provides much higher capacity, suggesting that the infrastructure could support significantly more concurrent requests if the application-level constraints were relaxed.
